The good news is: You’re getting a free dinner. The bad news is: You’re now racking your brain for last-minute hostess gifts . Buying something nice for a host is a tricky affair—there’s no expectation to spend a lot of money, nor is there one to bring something other than a bottle of wine, really, but the people pleasers among us will resonate with this list (and our housewarming gifts write-up).

In our search for the most memorable and thoughtful gifts to buy when you’ve been invited anywhere, we located a range of fail-safe favorites: cordial glasses (a small cut above wine glasses), scented candles you really want for yourself, linen coasters—basically everything but the finishing salt (though that would’ve been a great addition…). Whether it’s a Christmas feast, a movie night, or just a casual aperitivo hour, stick with this roundup for the perfect hostess gift ideas.

The name says it all—showing up with one of these gifts is all but a guarantee you’ll be getting invited to every function to come. You won’t find benchwarmers anywhere on this list; every item in this category is truly an MVP. Highlights include a cookbook, a box of chocolate truffles, and an AD-team favorite in serveware from Lazy Jamie.

Those who suffer from short-term memory loss rely heavily on Amazon Prime memberships for that two-day turnaround. If you’re down to the wire and still in need of something thoughtful to deliver to your gracious host, these gifts will arrive as early as the next day. Throw a bow on these and no one will know you nearly forgot about your plans.

There’s no getting around it—this social situation is going to be weird for you, at least for the first 20 minutes. These unique hostess gifts will usher you into the in-group expeditiously, especially since they can use them as soon as this evening for serving dinner or dessert. If you secured an invite to their upstate cabin or beach cottage, you need to get something nice. Bring a set of waffle kitchen towels, a stoneware jar for the pantry, or a marbled guest book for the entryway to underscore the log cabin vibe, and they’ll be smitten. In no time, you’ll be invited back up there by yourself to watch the dog and water the plants, wearing a muddy pair of Hunter boots with a dwindling social life back in the city.

Oui, oui! Maybe your hosts tried their hardest to find a Paris-style apartment in New York City (only to discover the truly authentic ones lacked an AC unit). And while they can’t wander around Le Marais on the daily, a very French pepper mill and an upgraded knife set for their cheese board might help scratch the itch. We left the escargot forks off just in case you didn’t want to encourage that type of appetizer.

Maybe they don’t drink anymore…or maybe they don’t drink any less. Even if you received a last-minute invite, it’s always good form to bring a bottle of wine, an aperitif, or something to the dinner party. Lucky for you, we found related options that’ll show your hosts you were thinking of them—pieces for accentuating their bar cart or tabletop, like a tortoise print wine key or a fresh set of glasses.

Making a pit stop to your partner’s parents this holiday season? Armor yourself with an arsenal of thoughtful gift ideas to solidify your status as their favorite bonus child. Cut flowers send someone looking for a vase, but a beaded lily never needs one. If you’re visiting their country home in New England, an elegant, coastal-inspired Serena and Lily throw will fit the vibe perfectly.

The invite may say, “Your presence is the only gift required,” but we’re inclined to bring a little something anyway. Whether it’s a casual get-together before everyone leaves town or your friend’s annual bash with a strict dress code, we’re here to tout a few gifting options that are more festive than a holiday card. For the statement maker who is never seen without a sequin, perhaps a cordial coupe made for a tiny cosmo? If your host is a bit more low-key, you can never go wrong with a bit of chrome or a hand towel set from Autumn Sonata.

Opening their living room or guest room to you is no small gesture. Show your appreciation with something that gives a little back to their home: A replacement for their favorite candle, a set of teas to help them unwind, or an inspirational coffee table tome to add to their precariously stacked collection. With one of these thoughtful items in tow, we’re sure you’ll be welcomed back with open arms any time there’s a concert in town.

#4735. Christina Applegate ‘Not Happy at All’ After Learning She Was Misdiagnosed With MS

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Christina Applegate shared an unexpected health update on her return to the MeSsy podcast with co-host Jamie-Lynn Sigler.

The two actors have detailed their experiences with multiple sclerosis (MS), a neurological disorder that can lead to debilitating symptoms affecting daily functioning and quality of life.

Applegate, 54, has been raising awareness about the condition since her initial diagnosis in 2021.

In two podcast episodes released October 20, Applegate revealed that doctors had told her she was misdiagnosed with MS.

“She came into my room and said, ‘Congratulations, you don’t have MS,’ ” Applegate said as she fought back tears. “I was, like, not happy at all. Everybody else was so happy.”

The “Anchorman” and “Dead to Me” actor explained that her symptoms have continued to worsen, leaving her without an explanation for what she’s experiencing as doctors investigate the cause.

Being misdiagnosed with MS is relatively common. Applegate’s revelation highlights a difficult reality for people living with unexplained symptoms resembling MS. Her experience raises questions about how MS is diagnosed, why misdiagnoses may occur, and what people can do when their symptoms don’t match their diagnosis.

While MS can be difficult to diagnose, an accurate diagnosis can help people with the condition gain access to appropriate treatment. A misdiagnosis, on the other hand, may lead to unnecessary interventions and medication, and take an emotional toll over time.

“MS can be challenging to diagnose because there is no single test that confirms it in every case,” said Steve Allder, MD, consultant neurologist at Re:Cognition Health.

“An incorrect diagnosis can have significant consequences. Someone incorrectly diagnosed with MS may experience considerable anxiety, undergo unnecessary investigations, or receive treatments with potential risks and side effects. Equally, if MS is missed, treatment may be delayed, potentially allowing further neurological damage,” Allder told Healthline.

A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis underscores that MS misdiagnoses remain a concern.

Research suggests that around 15% of people diagnosed with MS may actually have another condition.

However, estimates vary across studies, with some reporting rates ranging from 5–41%.

While an accurate diagnosis can guide patients toward appropriate treatment, a mistaken one may lead to unnecessary medication, emotional distress, and years of uncertainty.

New diagnostic guidelines offer hope for greater accuracy, but they also raise important questions about how doctors can adequately distinguish MS from other conditions.

“Research has shown that MS can be both overdiagnosed and underdiagnosed,” Allder said.

“Diagnosis relies on a combination of symptoms, neurological examination, MRI findings, and sometimes, additional tests. It is also important to recognize that diagnoses can evolve as new evidence emerges. As neurologists, we must remain open to revisiting a diagnosis when symptoms or test results do not fit, ensuring patients receive appropriate treatment and support.”

MS symptoms may vary widely and overlap with several other conditions. These may include:

Because these conditions share certain features with MS, healthcare professionals should consider a patient’s full clinical profile rather than relying on a single symptom or scan.

“MS can cause numbness, tingling, muscle weakness, visual disturbances, balance problems, and fatigue. However, these symptoms are not unique to the condition,” Allder said.

“For example, numbness and tingling may indicate peripheral neuropathy, sometimes associated with diabetes or vitamin B12 deficiency. Weakness or altered sensation may result from a trapped nerve or spinal cord compression. Migraines can cause visual disturbances and sensory symptoms, while inner-ear disorders may affect balance,” he continued.

Allder noted that fatigue is particularly nonspecific and may be associated with:

He explained that, as a neurologist, he considers the pattern, duration, and progression of symptoms alongside examination findings.

“No single symptom automatically indicates MS. A thorough assessment is essential to identify the underlying cause and ensure the patient receives appropriate treatment,” he said.

There is no single test that definitively confirms every case of MS.

Diagnosis typically involves reviewing symptoms, conducting neurological examinations, and evaluating MRI scans and laboratory results.

MRI findings may be tricky to interpret. Some white-matter spots resemble MS lesions but may result from migraine, aging, or other conditions. Misapplying diagnostic criteria or overlooking alternative explanations can also lead to mistakes.

“MRI abnormalities alone do not confirm MS,” Allder said. “The diagnosis must be based on the overall clinical picture, with alternative explanations carefully considered.”

Research also suggests that MS misdiagnosis rates may differ by sex.

Research shows females are 2.1 times more likely to be misdiagnosed with MS than males, highlighting the potential for diagnostic bias and differences in how symptoms are evaluated.

The updated MS diagnostic criteria published in 2025 offer a framework for improving diagnosis.

The updated guidelines introduce several important changes.

For instance, the optic nerve (the nerve connecting the eye to the brain) is now included as a fifth anatomical location for assessing evidence of MS.

The revised criteria also include new MRI biomarkers, such as the central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions. These features can help doctors distinguish MS-related abnormalities from other conditions.

These changes may help doctors diagnose MS earlier and more accurately.

If you experience persistent or recurring neurological symptoms, seek medical advice. Your doctor can assess your symptoms and, if applicable, refer you to a neurologist.

Sudden weakness, vision loss, or difficulty speaking requires urgent medical assessment, Allder said.

“Depending on the findings, investigations may include MRI scans of the brain and spinal cord, blood tests, and, in some cases, a lumbar puncture,” Allder noted.

“It is important that results are interpreted alongside symptoms and examination findings, as no single test should determine the diagnosis in isolation.”

Allder said that if you’re unsure about a diagnosis, you can ask your neurologist what evidence supports it and whether alternative health conditions have been considered.

“A second opinion or follow-up assessment may be appropriate. The priority is an accurate diagnosis that leads to the right treatment and support,” Allder said.

#4734. Everyone wants an electric pickup truck. I want more electric 125cc motorcycles

If you follow the EV industry in North America, you’d be forgiven for thinking that the future of transportation revolves around electric SUVs and pickups. Every week seems to bring another teaser from a startup promising to reinvent the family car or truck. The latest electric SUVs, “coming soon” tiny trucks, lifestyle trucks, modular trucks, etc. Companies like Slate, TELO, and countless others have generated plenty of excitement, even if many of them still have everything left to prove.

Don’t get me wrong – I hope they succeed. We need more affordable electric vehicles. But after spending nearly two decades covering a specific part of the electric-vehicle space and a good chunk of that time traveling around the world to see how people actually get around, I can’t help but wonder if we’re chasing the wrong prize here.

Because while the West keeps trying to electrify pickup trucks and SUVs, much of the world has already settled on a far more sensible transportation appliance.

Western readers often think of a sedan as the world’s “normal” or “sensible” vehicle.

But go traveling almost anywhere in Asia, and that illusion disappears in about five minutes.

The roads are filled with Honda Clicks and CG125s, Hero Splendors, Yamaha NMAXs and YBR125s, and countless other small-displacement motorcycles. They carry workers to jobs, students to school, families to dinner, and every imaginable cargo in between.

They’re the delivery vans. They’re the commuter cars. They’re grocery getters, family transportation, and work trucks. And perhaps more importantly, they transport hundreds of millions of people every single day.

You don’t have to spend long in places like the Philippines before realizing something else: these aren’t really “motorcycle cultures.” They’re just transportation cultures. People ride these machines because they make sense.

And I’ve done it myself to see what all the fuss was about. Sure, I’m an e-motorcycle guy through and through. But I’ve been there to ride a mile in their motorcycle sandals, and so I get it.

Even so, having had one cheek on each saddle, I still have to think there’s a better way than the tried-and-true 125cc combustion engine motorcycles that have become the workhorse of much of the world.

The extreme proliferation of small motorcycles is what makes the current electric motorcycle market feel so strange. If there were ever a class of gasoline vehicle that batteries are already capable of replacing, it’s the 125cc combustion engine motorcycle.

These bikes aren’t demanding. They generally produce a modest 10-15 hp (8–11 kW) of power. They cruise comfortably around 45-60 mph (70-100 km/h). Most riders travel relatively short daily distances measured in dozens of miles, not hundreds.

A modern electric motorcycle with a 4-6 kWh battery can comfortably accomplish those same tasks while offering smoother acceleration, quieter operation, lower maintenance, and dramatically lower operating costs.

Unlike replacing a heavy-duty pickup truck that tows livestock trailers across Montana, replacing a 125cc commuter bike is already well within today’s battery technology. In many ways, it’s one of the easiest transportation sectors to electrify.

Instead, North America’s electric motorcycle market developed in an odd direction.

We have electric bicycles, and those are great for urban commuters. But then we jump almost straight to premium electric motorcycles costing $15,000 to $25,000. The practical middle has remained surprisingly sparse.

The ONYX RCR became something of a cult favorite by proving there was genuine demand for lightweight, motorcycle-like electric transportation without superbike performance.

Ryvid’s Anthem pushed further, adding highway capability while still remaining approachable and relatively affordable.

The new LiveWire S4 Honcho also feels like an encouraging step toward a lighter, more practical electric motorcycle instead of another oversized premium machine.

Even Infinite Machine’s Olto, while occupying a slightly different category, demonstrates growing interest in practical urban electric two-wheelers that prioritize transportation over headline horsepower.

These companies are proving something important: People don’t necessarily need 100 horsepower. Many simply need transportation.

Don’t misunderstand me. Electric pickup trucks absolutely have their place. Electric SUVs do too.

But we’ve spent the last decade pouring enormous engineering effort into electrifying some of the least energy-efficient passenger vehicles on the road.

Meanwhile, we’ve largely ignored one of the most efficient gasoline vehicle classes humanity has ever created.

A typical 125cc combustion engine motorcycle can already achieve fuel economy approaching or exceeding 100 mpg (2.35 liters/100 km). An electric equivalent becomes almost absurdly efficient.

We’re talking roughly 4-6 kWh per 100 kilometers (62 miles) – just a fraction of the energy consumed even by many compact electric cars. I once did the math, and a light electric motorcycle can travel 10,000 km (roughly 6,000 miles) for around $160 in electricity. Basically, your electrical bill doesn’t even notice when you own an electric motorcycle. Charging it simply doesn’t move the needle.

Instead of asking how we can fit ever-larger battery packs into increasingly larger SUVs and trucks, perhaps we should also be asking how many trips don’t need a large vehicle in the first place.

Transportation statistics across much of the developed world tell a familiar story.

Most trips involve one person. Maybe there’s also a backpack in the mix. Maybe there are some groceries getting picked up on the way home. Occasionally, there’s another passenger.

Those things are exactly what small motorcycles have been doing around the world for decades.

I recently spent some time in the Philippines, where I watched motorcycles carrying impossible-looking loads every day. Entire families would ride together. Construction materials. Furniture. Livestock. I saw two pigs on a 125cc bike, I kid you not. I’ve seen even crazier things in Thailand.

Again, I’m certainly not advocating that we adopt some of those practices in the West – there are obvious safety considerations – but it demonstrates just how incredibly capable these machines can be.

Even within normal Western expectations, a 125cc-class motorcycle is capable of handling an astonishing percentage of daily transportation needs.

This is where discussions about motorcycles often become unnecessarily polarized.

No, motorcycles aren’t ideal in every situation. Yes, heavy rain exists. Snow exists. Families with multiple children exist. Long interstate road trips exist.

Nobody is suggesting a 125cc electric motorcycle should replace every car.

If a household can replace even half of its daily driving with a lightweight electric motorcycle, that’s already a massive reduction in energy consumption, congestion, parking demand, and transportation costs.

Transportation doesn’t have to be all-or-nothing. So enough with this “but what if it rains?” stuff. Either put on a jacket that day or drive your car. But for the majority of the trips each year you take where it’s not raining, you could have done it in a much more efficient (and fun) way.

One of the biggest conversations surrounding EV adoption is charging. But smaller electric motorcycles barely participate in that problem. A 4-5 kWh battery charges overnight from an ordinary household outlet. The outlet you plug your laptop charger into is basically the equivalent of a Level 2 public charger for an e-motorcycle – that’s how fast it is.

DC fast charging isn’t really necessary on a light electric motorcycle. There’s no need for an expensive home charger. There’s no massive battery pack. Just plug it in before bed and wake up with a battery that’s been fully charged and waiting on you for hours already.

And if you want to go wild, there are swappable battery networks like Gogoro in Taiwan or Vammo in South America that can make charging unnecessary.

Another advantage rarely discussed is intimidation. Many people don’t want a 600 lb (270 kg) motorcycle producing superbike acceleration. They want something approachable, something lightweight, maneuverable, easy to park, and easy to live with.

That’s exactly why 125cc motorcycles became so successful globally.

Electric versions preserve all of those advantages while making them even easier to ride thanks to instant torque and the absence of clutch work. Many of them even come with reverse mode, making them easier to park and wiggle around even on hilly terrain.

One reason Europe has seen more progress here is that the regulatory framework already exists.

Manufacturers regularly market bikes as “125cc equivalents,” and consumers immediately understand what that means.

Licensing systems and insurance companies recognize the category. It’s a mature transportation class.

North America, by comparison, often treats motorcycles as either recreational toys or large-displacement touring machines. We’ve largely forgotten that much of the world simply sees them as transportation.

Ironically, younger riders may already be showing us the way forward.

The explosion in popularity of Sur Ron-style electric motorcycles and lightweight e-motos demonstrates that younger generations are perfectly willing to embrace two-wheeled electric transportation.

Not everyone buying those bikes is looking for motocross. Many simply enjoy the freedom, accessibility, affordability, and fun that come with traveling on two wheels.

Rather than dismissing that trend, perhaps we should recognize it as an opportunity. Today’s recreational rider often becomes tomorrow’s commuter.

If someone discovers they enjoy getting around on an electric two-wheeler, moving from a lightweight e-moto to a practical 125cc-equivalent commuter becomes a much smaller leap than convincing someone to abandon their car entirely.

One observation has stuck with me after so many years of covering the electric vehicle industry and traveling through countries where motorcycles dominate daily life. The West has spent years trying to electrify the largest, heaviest, and least efficient vehicles on our roads. Meanwhile, we’ve paid surprisingly little attention to electrifying the vehicle that already moves much of humanity every single day.

In Europe at least, there's a cliff between a pedal ebike, which anyone can ride without any pre planning, and a motorcycle which needs passing a specific test, taxing, taking out insurance and wearing safety gear. Even people with car licences need to take driving lessons and the test. It means you can't just step on a motorcycle when it makes sense you need potentially months of planning. It's much easier just to take a car you're already licensed for.

I’m not arguing that everyone should ride a motorcycle. And I’m certainly not arguing that cars no longer have an important place.

But perhaps we’ve underestimated just how many people could benefit from something in between.

Not just an electric bicycle, and not just a $25,000 electric motorcycle. Just an honest, practical, affordable electric equivalent of the vehicle that already keeps much of the world moving.

Because if we’re serious about accelerating electric transportation, maybe the future isn’t another electric pickup truck. Maybe it’s finally giving the world’s favorite motorcycle an electric motor.

Micah Toll is a personal electric vehicle enthusiast, battery nerd, and author of the Amazon #1 bestselling books DIY Lithium Batteries, DIY Solar Power, The Ultimate DIY Ebike Guide and The Electric Bike Manifesto.

The e-bikes that make up Micah’s current daily drivers are the $999 Lectric XP 2.0, the $1,095 Ride1Up Roadster V2, the $1,199 Rad Power Bikes RadMission, and the $3,299 Priority Current. But it’s a pretty evolving list these days.

#4733. There’s No Irony in The Armored League. Only Steel.

Welcome to NYC’s extremely violent, surprisingly wholesome new combat scene.

“THERE’S A LOT more work to do,” Damion DiGrazia muses, as 30 or so individuals spread themselves out across the gymnasium at the Manhattanville Community Center in Harlem. A pair of double doors swings lazily back and forth, marking a procession of students and the boxes they carry. DiGrazia leans against the wall, dressed in a red polo and khaki trousers, watching his small community unpack and ready itself for training.

The class does not have a format in the traditional sense. There is no lantern-jawed instructor with a whistle and a clipboard. No snap of uniforms in sync with the rhythm of a kata. There is not even, as far as I could tell, a formal warm-up. Instead, the room seems to have its own sense of internal order.

A group forms around the pieces of armor to begin the painstaking process of polishing and assessing each one for damage or repairs. Some—a breastplate, maybe a set of greaves—are singled out and ferried to a corner, where three individuals sit, cross-legged, and carefully hammer out the dents.

Ropes are thrown over the basketball hoops, and as soon as they land, students appear and begin practicing striking drills with blunted steel weapons. There are, admittedly, a lot of people with weapons. It’s a little surreal at first. When you encounter a fighter in full armor with a sword and buckler or a mace, there is a sense of visual cohesion. It is an entirely different matter to pass a fighter in cutoff denim and a T-shirt practicing elegant, sweeping strikes with an axe.

At the back of the room, the mats find their way into a rectangle, and small scrimmages begin with foam swords and shields. The training takes on its own rhythm; newer members train with foam swords and shields around the edges of the room, while the more seasoned fighters, now sporting what appear to be hockey helmets with face masks, begin grappling practice at its center. Everyone seems to know where they need to be and what they need to do.

It’s taken a long time to get here—years, actually, 13 of them, to be precise. After serving in the military, DiGrazia traces a path through Columbia University, then Harvard, before landing a job at Morgan Stanley. Finding the rhythm of corporate life increasingly dull, he sought relief through extreme sports. DiGrazia started with the classics: marathons, ultramarathons, scuba diving, skydiving, martial arts. But nothing really stuck; he was always chasing something else. That is, until a happy accident. DiGrazia tried what he thought was going to be “full-contact” LARPing (live-action role-playing), but found the experience less than fulfilling: “You couldn't punch people, couldn't grapple people, couldn't kick people, nothing,” DiGrazia says. The participants were wearing plastic armor, and a hit to the leg saw fighters taking a theatrical knee and swiping at their opponents. At the end of the practice, however, DiGrazia found himself sticking around, commiserating with another fighter, Zorikh, whom he credits as starting his journey along a path that would lead to him founding Gladiators NYC, and laying the groundwork for The Armored League.

Modern armored combat has a longer history in Europe, and DiGrazia found himself bouncing all over the continent, fighting in Poland or next to a castle in Spain. If you wanted to fight in armor, Eastern Europe was where you had to go. Stateside, the early days were decidedly underground and homebrew. Your options were more limited: small groups of fighters met in parking lots and cornfields. Orlando Mendez, one of the founding members of Gladiators NYC, remembers “a lot of horse arenas.” They were one of the few places you could throw someone into a wall without complaint. It was a sport that grew anywhere it could find space. Jason Puerta, owner of Golden Ring Combat, a West Coast armored combat group, recalls regularly fighting on the lawns of a corporate campus after securing the bemused blessing of the local security outfit. It wasn’t quite Fight Club—new members were always welcome (and still are), and people were encouraged to talk about it. Instead, the group could be said to be self-selective: “You either got the hang of it, or you just turned in your armor at the end of the day,” DiGrazia recalls. There were few rules, no weight divisions, and no weapon classes.

In these early years, the attrition rate was high. DiGrazia estimates about half of the participants quit within weeks. Even when he first secured the community center and started spreading the word about classes, he remembers sitting on a bench in the gym, staring at the doors, waiting for someone, anyone, to come to a class. Eventually, they did.

The free classes, access to equipment, loaner armor, and the open exhibition matches in New York’s Central Park—all of these, he believes, must remain core elements of the community and the sport. Gladiators NYC also has a nonprofit arm called “Santa’s Knights” where armored knights go door to door during the holidays and deliver presents to children. His commitment to this approach has not come without difficulties. DiGrazia once partnered with a martial arts school whose owner forbade him from sponsoring students who could not afford the $30 class fee. That school closed during COVID.

Technically, the sport can trace its roots back to the 14th century, when knights, foot soldiers, and men-at-arms would practice combat using dull steel weapons and a mixture of soft and plate armor. It was a way to hone their skills in times of peace. The fundamentals of the practice remain in a number of combat sports to this day, but one need only watch a bout of Olympic fencing (or “pointy tag” as Mendez described it) to realize the distance traveled. The Armored League, however, doesn’t seek a return to its medieval origins or even to the stringently historically accurate expressions, which tend to dominate in Europe. When pressed about this, DiGrazia gives an exasperated sigh: “I don't want some librarian walking around looking with a fucking magnifying glass on everybody's goddamn rivet. Leave us alone. Let's have a good time.” The aim is to bring the spectacle and joy to new audiences.

Even if, at first, you cannot follow the scoring, the fights are pure melodrama. Like any combat sport, the fighters’ stats are announced as they enter the ring—with one key distinction: their weight includes their suit of armor. Short of a quirk, it communicates the impact of the sport in a more visceral way: when a pair of combatants crash to the ground or bounce off the chain-link fencing, that’s close to 600 pounds of flesh and steel set in ballistic motion.

Bouts are divided into three to five one-minute rounds. Points are awarded based on strikes—where they land and how hard. Basic, clean strikes with weapons, shields, or fists get a base number of points. Meanwhile headshots, two-handed weapon strikes, and slugging a downed opponent get you even more. The bouts are judged by a panel set to one side of the ring, while a pair of counters runs frantically around the perimeter counting strikes.

There are comparatively few rules beyond some basic safety precautions: no stabbing or thrusting; no stomping; no strikes at the inner elbows, armpits, or the backs of knees; no slashing at the neck; and no submissions. Save for these, anything goes, and this adds to the thrill of the fights. Fighters are also not limited to their weapons, and in some cases, they will stand and trade blows like boxers. Though all of the serious fighters have broad and varied martial arts backgrounds—and training approaches—there's a roughly consistent path that leads to The Armored League. Snatches of Muay Thai knee strikes, judo sweeps, classical boxing, escrima, and BJJ are all visible in the blur of limbs, steel, and weapons. One can only imagine how the “librarians” would feel about that.

Strikes may come in flurries or great arcs, but most are hard enough to send sparks flying off the helmets. There is a marshal in the ring with the fighters, notably unarmored save for a yellow flag that’s mainly used to break the fighters up at the end of each round, which frequently ends in a tangle of armor and weapons on the floor of the ring.

There are two elements that, despite the passage of centuries, have not changed: cost and danger. Historians are divided on the exact conversion rate between 1400 and today, and most put it in terms of wages. They quote the cost of a full set of armor at somewhere between 12 and 18 months of pay. What’s universally agreed upon is that arms and armor were (and remain) anything but cheap. A full suit—then, as now—weighs anywhere from 60 to 80 pounds.

This century, prices start at around $5,000 and climb precipitously with customization. It can take anywhere from a few weeks to a year for delivery. Most participants build their suits over time as they are drawn deeper into the sport.

Building a full set is not easy. A cursory search online will lead you to a number of pages, which might appear to offer armor, but these sites are largely focused on cosplayers or LARPers. That armor will certainly hold together for a walk through Comic-Con, but it will do little to protect from a real blow. The handful of armorers still working today have long wait lists. Puerta notes that despite this, the communal nature of the sport means that much of the armor is passed down or traded between the combatants: as someone upgrades or hangs up their helmet, the armor finds its way into a new pair of hands or onto a new person’s shoulders. At Gladiators NYC, fighters who graduate from the classes, from “softs” (padded armor), and wish to try their hand at the real thing, can borrow pieces from Gladiators NYC’s own armory.

Amongst the current fighters who regularly participate in Armored League matches, almost all fight in custom armor. The suits must adhere to certain safety standards—thickness of steel, comprehensive eye protection, etc. But beyond that, there’s ample room for self-expression.

For example, Abeid “Mando” Mitchell fights in comparatively minimalist and lightweight armor and is readily recognizable by his distinctive helmet, which was made in the style of the Mandalorian from Star Wars. Luke “The Red Knight of Brooklyn” has assembled what he refers to as “a sporting replica” of 1480s armor in keeping with his own, more classical concerns.

Despite the care and attention each fighter devotes to their own armor, at all of the matches I attended, I saw weapons traded freely, shields swapped, even gauntlets lent. For as much violence as there is inside of a 60-second round, there is an equal, if not greater, level of care at the bell. The armor is not just for show; it’s for safety. Combatants want to win as much as they want to ensure their opponent walks off the field under their own power. It’s a fine balance, and as Mendez put it, “once you put on the armor and you get your ass beat a couple of times,” everybody is basically friends.

Nevertheless, it takes a toll. Puerta told me a story of how he almost lost his left eye when the tip of a sword slipped through the bars of his helmet. Others relayed stories of being crushed in a melee and of “helmet terrors” where breathing heavily in the confines of a helmet causes a buildup of carbon dioxide and creates a sensation similar to drowning.

What does the future look like? In my time with the League and Gladiators NYC, I sensed I was watching a sport in its adolescence. It is a league and community that seems to blink in the stark light of its own success and rapidly growing audience. Social media has made it easier for these once disparate communities to connect; the cornfields and horse rinks have been parlayed into an Octagon at the Melrose Ballroom in Queens or a showcase at a theater in Times Square. The bleachers that once held a smattering of friends and family have shifted into crowds drawn from all walks of life—at the sold-out show in Queens, the lines stretched around the block and some people waited an hour just to get into the venue. The Central Park exhibition matches, which happen every second Saturday of the month, have begun to draw crowds that can number over a thousand.

DiGrazia and his merry band have come a long way from the leaner years, when they struggled to find space to practice, the years when they fought in the parking lots of regional hotels in the Midwest or in the summer heat on the boardwalk in Coney Island.

Still, there is, for now, little to no money in this sport. The community, and the fighters too, all have day jobs. They are PhD students, fitness instructors, photographers, and graphic designers. One manages a magic and costume shop. Again, Fight Club springs to mind, as each goes about their day job, bearing the marks of a Thursday brawl or a weekend match, one can only wonder if anyone sees a bruise sticking out of a shirt sleeve and stops to ask just where it came from.

#4732. I Found the 11 Best Running Shoes for Women for Every Type of Run

From trail running to marathons to daily training, our running shoe guide has a recommendation for every runner.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

LOW-IMPACT EXERCISES might be forever buzzy, but the running community is going stronger than ever. From 5Ks to marathons, lots of women are lacing up to go for a run and getting all the physical and mental health benefits that come with it. Data suggests running is great for everything from cardiovascular fitness to a healthier mindset, and it may even lower your risk of eight major diseases, making it a solid fitness habit to get into. And then there’s the fact that running makes you feel like you’ve accomplished something amazing (because you have).

As a former competitive runner who still throws down high mileage (50 to 60 miles weekly), I’ve learned the right footwear is crucial for allowing you to continue to pound the pavement, and selecting the right kind of running shoe is important, too. The best running shoes for women provide support and cushioning, with the perfect level of fit to help you forget about your footwear while you run.

While you can skimp on some fitness gear, a quality pair of running shoes is an important investment, according to Melissa Lockwood, DPM, a podiatrist at Heartland Foot and Ankle Associates in Bloomington, Illinois “I am very much in the camp of paying for a really good pair of running shoes,” she says. “It can help really minimize injury in the future.” (Still, if you’re on a tight budget or just want to save a buck, these are our favorite cheap running shoes.)

But, before taking the plunge on racking up miles, it’s important to figure out what kind of heel-to-toe drop, toe box, stability, cushioning, and heel stack is best for you. Finding the perfect running shoes involves understanding how specific design elements impact your comfort, performance, and overall experience.

There is no right or wrong, as everyone has different needs (and those needs for running shoes differ from walking shoes), but we'll go over the most important factors to consider when shopping for running shoes.

Hoka does it right when it comes to a durable, high-quality shoe—specifically the Clifton 11, which was released in July 2026 in tandem with the higher-performance-oriented Clifton Pro. The Clifton family has been a crowd pleaser in the running community and amongst WH editors for a long time, and with good reason.

The Clifton 11 is considered one of the brand’s most versatile running shoes, making it a good fit for everyone from beginners to seasoned pros. WH style editor Shannon Zitz says her feet never felt fatigued while she was testing this shoe, even with plantar fasciitis. “There’s technically a rocker shape built into the sole, but it's subtle enough that I barely noticed it—instead, my stride just felt smooth and natural whether I was walking or running,” she says.

The Clifton 11 has an eight-millimeter heel-to-toe drop to help alleviate pressure on the plantar fascia, and the brand shaved off almost half an ounce from the weight of the model’s previous version, the Clifton 10, primarily through weight-saving revisions to the shoe’s upper. This was the primary change, with Hoka keeping the midsole that we know and love the same.

These shoes offer maximum cushioning you’ll feel—the same EVA foam found in the Bondi 9 without the extra bulk. Just be aware that these don’t offer any stability innovations for flat feet, which is especially essential if you’re prone to overpronation. As for fit, the toe box does run narrow, but luckily, wide sizing is available.

Read More: Hoka Clifton 11 vs. Hoka Clifton Pro

On has built an empire out of its highly cushioned Cloudmonster line. But its most cushioned shoe of all is the Cloudmonster 3 Hyper, an impressively bouncy sneaker that’ll make you feel like a gazelle bounding down the street.

It’s generally accepted that the more cushioning a shoe has, the heavier its weight (because of all that foam packed into the midsole). But the On Cloudmonster 3 Hyper manages to deliver a highly cushioned shoe in a relatively lightweight 7.5 oz package. The result is a next-level energy return that feels like it’s propelling you forward with each step.

This sneaker has a soft, breathable upper to minimize foot sweat, along with a highly padded heel collar that lowers the risk of rubbing. I’ve worn a lot of running shoes, and that heel collar may be the thickest I’ve ever seen. There’s a nice, roomy toe box, too.

While there’s a lot to love about the Cloudmonster 3 Hyper, it’s not perfect. This shoe’s $220 price tag puts it out of reach for many, and the tongue is on the thin side (not a deal-breaker, but some people prefer something more padded). Still, if you have the budget for it and like to feel like you’re running on actual clouds, this is a solid choice.

Think of a daily trainer as the chameleon of the running shoe world. This sneaker needs to be able to be durable enough for regular use, comfortable, and versatile enough to handle higher mileage along with speedier runs. The Adidas Adizero Evo SL was designed with all of that in mind, serving up a highly adaptable shoe that works for nearly everyone. That’s probably why this shoe keeps landing on the feet of runners all over the place.

The Adizero Evo SL has a soft, bouncy feel underfoot and plenty of energy return thanks to Adidas’ proprietary Lightstrike Pro foam packed into the midsole. It’s also relatively lightweight, clocking in at just under 8 oz. The shoe’s peppy sensation and slight rocker shape support your stride but don’t push you forward in a way that feels unnatural.

This sneaker has an engineered mesh upper to let your feet breathe, even when you’re clocking some serious mileage. This shoe has a slightly tapered toe box, which isn’t for everyone. The outsole is also a little flat and isn’t the grippiest you’ll find, but road runners are unlikely to have an issue. While you’re probably not choosing a running shoe based on looks alone, it doesn’t hurt that the Adizero Evo SL looks sleek.

The best shoe for recovery runs is a total workhorse, delivering enough stability and cushioning to keep you comfortable as you move along at a moderate pace. The Brooks Ghost Max 3 is up for the challenge, with a wide, stable base and supportive feel to take the pressure off your joints.

This isn’t a stability shoe, per se—it won’t work to correct your stride—but it still creates a sense like you’re not going to roll an ankle or have any other gait issues as you pound the pavement. The Ghost Max 3 is a heavier shoe, although I haven’t noticed any fatigue or extra drag in it. But this sneaker holds up well to high-volume running. I wear this regularly and have never noticed any durability issues.

The Ghost Max 3 features nitrogen-infused DNA Loft v3 foam for support and cushioning. However, it won’t give you a sinking-in feel and there is limited energy return, which could be a pro or con, depending on what you’re after. This sneaker also has a jacquard mesh upper that feels a little softer than many other running shoes out there. The Ghost Max 3 provides plenty of room, from the midfoot to the toe box, making it a good fit for people with wider feet. Just don’t plan to do any speed work in this shoe—it’s a little too heavy for that.

It's clear that Lululemon’s Wildfeel was designed by people who actually do trail running. It has features you want in a trail running shoe beyond just good grip.

There’s a knitted sock-like upper that molds to your foot to keep out pebbles and other debris, along with a toe bumper to protect your feet over rugged terrain. I took these shoes on several runs over a rocky trail near my house, along with a few beach runs, and was impressed at how well it kept the stuff outside from getting into my shoe.

The Wildfeel has a dual-density midsole, which means that it helps give you a feeling of moving forward when you're going up hills and absorbs impact when you’re going down.

Like many other Lululemon shoes, the toe box runs a little narrow. My heel slipped around a little when I first wore these shoes, although that’s pretty common in a trail shoe, and it got better with time and more wear.

There’s a wide range of shoes that consider themselves “stability” sneakers, but the Hoka Arahi 8 does a solid job correcting your stride with each step without being annoying. Many stability shoes are clunky and heavy, but the Arahi 8 manages to be lightweight at just 7.7 oz.

The Arahi 8 features a lot of changes from the previous version, the Arahi 7. This shoe uses special H-frame technology, featuring foam at the inner and outer foot, to deliver a more balanced support system. It’s roomy and comfortable, too. But this shoe is clearly not for everyone.

The level of stability is high, and that constant gait correction may feel like too much for some people. It also isn’t very responsive, so you’re not getting much back from your shoe with each stride other than security. (To be fair, though, that’s what people are usually after with a stability shoe.) Still, the Arahi 8 is impressively cushioned and very comfortable, whether you’re working your way through a long training session or just going out on a daily run.

Long runs require plenty of cushioning to support you along the way. The Nike Vomero Plus, which won the award for Best Cushioned Running Shoe in the 2026 Women’s Health Fitness Awards, is here to help. This shoe delivers a fun, bouncy feel that helps propel you as you rack up the miles.

The Vomero Plus has a roomy toe box and overall comfortable feel, serving up a shoe that makes long runs a little more seamless. That bounciness comes courtesy of Nike’s ZoomX foam, which is positioned along the length of the shoe. The engineered upper is crafted from yarn for a soft, breathable sensation.

The Vomero Plus provides a grippy outsole, making it perfect for the pavement. But if you’re looking for a stability shoe, the Vomero Plus isn’t it. Its high heel stack and bounciness is too much for that. But if you want a highly cushioned feel as you log some serious miles, this is an excellent choice.

The right race day shoe has the tough challenge of being supportive, cushiony, and lightweight, helping you to hit a PR without feeling like your footwear is holding you back. The New Balance FuelCell SuperComp Elite v5 is designed with longer-distance racers (think: half and marathon runners) in mind, but can still be an excellent choice for 5Ks and 10Ks thanks to its lightweight (6 oz) construction and solid energy return.

Let’s get this out of the way now: At $265, this is not a cheap shoe. With that, it’s unlikely to be a good investment for the occasional racer. But if your weekends are booked with road races, it’s worth at least considering.

This shoe delivers a locked-in feel, along with great traction to give you more confidence, even over wet surfaces. The roomy toe box and breathable upper also reinforce the FuelCell SuperComp Elite v5’s comfortable feel. This shoe is stable without sacrificing punchiness, helping you to feel supported as you stride. Just be aware that the midfoot and heel may feel a little too narrow for those with wider feet. But, luckily, this sneaker is available in wide widths, too.

Read More: Best Running Shoes for Plantar Fasciitis

The lululemon Beyondfeel running shoes truly live up to their name. They’re comfortable at the heels (and everywhere), with a heel stack that provides just the right amount of cushioning. It absorbs impact while still feeling responsive, especially during long runs. Plus, the cushioning around the ankle delivers security in every step.

The heel-to-toe drop is also a game changer—it really makes a difference for runners who heel-strike. Instead of feeling the usual jarring sensation from heel-striking, there are smooth transitions from each step. The bounce in the heel also makes it easier to maintain a steady stride without losing momentum, which is a huge benefit for runners who naturally land on their heels. The shoes guide feet to strike with the midfoot instead of the heel.

These shoes feel slightly bouncy while you run, and offer decent grip for trails and roads, making for a versatile running shoe. If you’re an overpronator, this isn’t the shoe for you—it doesn’t provide enough medial support (on the inside of the shoe). But it’s got plenty of features to make running a dream for heel strikers.

There’s a range in severity with overpronators, and what works for one won’t work for everyone. But the Asics Gel-Nimbus 28 does a solid job trying to please everyone in the overpronation camp. This shoe delivers a feel that’s not too soft or too firm, giving you the support and stability you need without feeling like you’re in a “special” shoe.

This shoe is lightweight for a stability shoe at 8.5 oz, making it good for most runs that don’t involve speed work. It also delivers a solid, locked-in sensation to make you feel secure with each step. The shoe’s OrthoLite sockliner also supports that cozier feel. The Gel-Nimbus 28 feels slightly springy underfoot, which is rare for a stability shoe. (Still, the overall effect isn’t very responsive compared to non-stability shoes.)

Asics in general tends to run narrow and the Gel-Nimbus 28 is no exception. If your feet tend to teeter between regular and wide sizes, you may want to consider hedging your bets and trying out a larger size.

The best shoe for speed work is very different from what you need for distance training or even race day. The Saucony Endorphin Azura is a lightweight (7.5 oz) shoe with a snappy feel that still manages to make you feel stable and locked in as you zip around.

The Saucony Endorphin Azura uses Pebax foam to create a responsive, bouncy feel, making you feel a little faster than usual. It also has a wide and stable base for added security during training. While it’s designed for speed, you can still comfortably wear this sneaker for longer runs and daily mileage. Just be aware that the shoe’s special SpeedRoll technology may feel slightly awkward at slower speeds.

The Endorphin Azura’s outsole features XT-900 rubber for a grippy feel underfoot, making you feel comfortable pushing the pace. Saucony shoes are known for a narrower fit, and the Endorphin Azura is no exception. If you have wider feet, it may be best to look elsewhere. (It unfortunately doesn’t come in wide sizes.)

Maximum Cushioning: This type of cushion feels amazingly plush and has excellent shock absorption, which is essential for long-distance running. While they’re designed to minimize the impact on the joints, they’re not the best for speed workouts unless the shoe has a lower heel-to-toe drop and some firmness.

Medium: If you want to balance speed with stability, medium cushioning is ideal. Too much cushioning can cause runners with flat feet to overpronate more from the bulkiness and softness. So, this type of cushioning is best if you want a more aligned gait.

This is the difference in height between the heel and front part (known as the forefoot) of the shoe. It can impact how your foot lands on the ground when you run. Low drops (0 to 4 mm) are flatter and encourage a natural running style where you land in the middle or front of your foot. They’re great if you like to feel close to the ground, enjoy trail running, or prefer a minimalist shoe design. Medium drop (5 to 8 mm) is a versatile option that offers mid-height and cushioning—this works well for most running styles. High drop (9 to 12 mm) tends to have more height in the heel to absorb impact (this is great for heel-strikers).

This is the height of the cushion under the heel. It’s measured from the outsole (the bottom of the shoe) to the insole (where your foot rests). Higher stacks offer more softness for long-distance running or for those who need less impact on the joints. Prioritizing this means sacrificing ground feel, and for some, that may feel unbalanced given the additional height.

Running shoes can provide a slew of benefits to suit your feet, but podiatrists stress the importance of getting a well-fitting shoe. “The shoe should fit your foot well and not cause any rubbing on the toes,” says Richard H. Graves, DPM, a podiatrist at Sol Foot & Ankle Centers in Long Beach, California “They should feel comfortable immediately upon putting them on and walking around.”

Consider these areas of the shoe when checking the fit:

Toe Box: This is the front part of the shoe where the toes sit. Toes spread naturally when you have extra room in the toe box, and this is especially important during long runs since feet can swell. But if the toe box is too big, it can lead to sliding and instability in the shoes.

Length: Since feet often swell from pounding pavement, it’s a good idea to have about a thumb’s width away from the tip of the shoe to your toe. If you’re unsure of your size, the best bet is to visit a running store to get properly fitted.

Arch Support: Those with flat feet and overpronators (when your foot lands on your outside heel and rolls inward) will want to look for shoes with enough firmness and high arch support to help keep feet aligned. Too much cushioning can create an unbalanced feeling, which can further aggravate pain. Those with neutral to high arches will have no issues wearing shoes with neutral support. Most shoes specify which arch type they accommodate, so make sure to read their product descriptions. And, definitely don’t wear shoes with no arch support—your feet need support.

The type of running workouts you plan to do will dictate elements like cushioning, support, and weight. More cushioning is often better with daily training and distance runs. You may also get away with a slightly heavier (but not too heavy) shoe, which usually means there’s more cushioning and stability. But shoes for speed work and race day tend to have less cushioning and a lighter weight, making it easier to move faster. For a deep-dive into the topic of running shoe selection, check out our story about how to figure out which type of running shoe you need.

A stability shoe can help correct gait issues like overpronation, which is when your foot rolls inward excessively when you run or walk. Not everyone needs a stability shoe, but some level of stability is important for reducing injury risk when you’re an overpronator. There are a few ways to tell if you overpronate, per Graves: Your feet appear to be rolling inward when you stand in a relaxed position and the heels of shoes you’ve worn are tilted inward.

You should switch out your running shoes every 300 to 500 miles. An easy way to maximize your shoe lifespan is to have a few pairs that you rotate between runs. Also, if you visually see them degrading, it's time to snag a new pair.

Running shoes can be washed in cold water in the washing machine with light detergent, or spot-cleaned with a sponge. But, you should never put your shoes in the dryer—they can shrink! Instead, let them air dry in the sun.

A simple at-home way to determine your arch type is the wet footprint test. You simply dip your foot in the water and step onto paper. If you see your entire foot, you have flat feet. Your foot will look like a comma if you have high arches, while a neutral arch will show slight elevation.

I’ve tested dozens of pairs of running shoes to determine which make the cut for the best running shoes for women. As a personal trainer, fitness writer, and runner with years of experience testing running shoes, I put each pair to the test during two-mile runs where I evaluated key performance factors such as cushioning, stability, comfort, support, traction, and responsiveness. I also considered how well the shoes supported my stride and whether or not they helped me maintain a consistent pace. Additionally, WH fitness editors provided feedback on select shoes they love to wear during training and racing.

#4731. New ID. AURA is the mainstream EV VW needs – but its software is the real story

Volkswagen built its global empire on the promise of affordable, accessible transportation, embodied by the iconic Type 1 Beetle. Now facing an existential crisis after a decades-long push upmarket, the automaker faces a reckoning – and a retreat back into affordable, mass-market electric sedans like the new FAW-VW ID. AURA L5 (and the software that powers it) might be exactly what VW needs to reach a new generation of buyers.

Like the Ford Model T, the original VW Type 1 Beetle was an engineering-led answer to a basic problem: making family transportation affordable and accessible to the masses. And regardless of how you feel about Elon Musk, the Tesla Model 3 has become the spiritual successor to those cars, bringing electric transportation to millions of mainstream drivers. As the Model 3 approaches its 11th year in public view, the recently revealed all-electric ID. AURA L5 and VW JETTA looks like it could be a compelling rival to the mainstream M3.

Co-developed by Volkswagen’s Chinese and German design teams and set to be built by the FAW-VW JV, the ID. AURA L5 is an Accord/Camry-sized electric family car a practical fastback-style rear hatch, frameless doors, and a claimed “84.4% usable floor-area ratio.” The power-operated hatchback opens its maw more than 70 degrees, revealing a 39″ wide opening that can handle groceries, luggage, golf clubs, pets, bodies – whatever you got.

Don’t take my word for it, though. This is the original text from the company’s press release (translated from Chinese by Google):

The ID. AURA L5 is a pure electric family sedan, jointly designed by Chinese and German design teams, and highly replicates the design essence of the ID. AURA concept car shown at the 2025 Shanghai Auto Show. Its short overhang and long wheelbase proportions create a sleek and flowing coupe-like stance, achieving a “usable floor area ratio” of 84.4%. The sides feature true frameless doors, semi-concealed door handles, and an electric hatchback tailgate with an opening angle exceeding 70°, and an opening width exceeding 1000 mm, greatly improving the convenience of loading and unloading large items, deeply integrating fastback aesthetics with practicality. Some models will be equipped with LiDAR and feature the Hyper Sense 8 end-to-end large model, making daily travel easier and more convenient for customers.

The production version of the ID. AURA L5 is expected to pack the same 155 kW (~208 hp) electric motors announced when the concept AURA L5 was first shown last year (battery specs were not released), and was shown as part of a broader product announcement of what VW Group China would be showcasing at this year’s China International Import Expo (CIIE). These include the first two models fully equipped with Volkswagen Group’s locally developed VEGA “integrated technology matrix” (read: software), and the Volkswagen Anhui intelligent pure electric “coupe” crossover.

The announcement coincides with reports from outlets like Autocar and Reuters that Volkswagen is evaluating whether to deploy its China-developed electrical architecture across the majority of its European markets.

“According to internal discussions confirmed by Group board member and Volkswagen brand CEO Thomas Schäfer,” reports Autocar’s Greg Kable, “up to 75% of the firm’s core models in Europe could eventually use the China Electronic Architecture.”

The Volkswagen Group has been struggling to deliver a software experience that resonates with customers. To their credit, they’re looking for outside help, spending billions of dollars on a software collaboration with EV startup Rivian for its upcoming electric truck brand Scout rather than going it alone. With billions of dollars and potential future of the company at stake, then, this seems like the most interesting bit of the announcement:

During the event, the immersive interactive experience exhibit “Digital Magic Cube,” which made its debut at last year’s China International Import Expo, will undergo an iterative upgrade to showcase the core strength of CEA (China Electronic Architecture), the software pillar of Volkswagen Group’s integrated self-developed technology matrix VEGA, to the attendees.

To date, CEA has enabled five new models from three joint ventures within the Volkswagen Group on a large scale, and software iterations have already been completed this year. CEA brings three core advantages to the Group’s new model lineup in China: intelligent accessibility, continuous upgrades, and safety redundancy. Through immersive interactive presentations, it provides consumers with the most intuitive experience. Empowered by the new AI R&D toolchain “C-Brain,” CEA introduces AI agents into software development, design, and engineering verification, enabling more flexible and efficient integration and innovation of vehicle intelligence capabilities, giving vehicles powerful thinking and perception abilities. Intelligent vehicles powered by CEA can better understand consumer needs, more efficiently create in-vehicle intelligent application scenarios, and better enhance digital intelligent safety redundancy, bringing Chinese consumers a new generation of intelligent mobility experience defined by Volkswagen standards

Sensible looking average car which should appeal to VW buyers provided the price, charging speed and range are right. Especially like that it has a hatch without being SUV shaped.

The show runs through November 10th, and we’ll be keeping an eye out for more details on the ID. AURA lineup and the Anhui intelligent pure electric coupe, including its powertrain, battery, and software specifications, as they become available.

#4730. Navigating the Unpredictable Ride of COPD

When COPD flare-ups affect breathing and health-related quality of life, ask about other treatment options.

HOOVES THUNDER AGAINST packed dirt as the bull bucks to the left and the rider leans right, tightening his grip on the rope. Just as he finds his balance, another sudden buck or turn can change the course of the ride.

The unexpected twists and turns of a bull ride may feel familiar to people living with inadequately controlled chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Not knowing when breathing challenges or a flare-up—a period when breathing becomes more difficult than usual that can last for several days—might occur can make everyday life feel unpredictable.

Mark H., 60, has experienced the challenges that can come with COPD since he was diagnosed in 2010. “COPD isn’t easy to navigate, and it can be a frightening condition to face,” he says. “I tried to ignore my diagnosis early on because I didn’t want to believe it, and I didn’t want to think about how it might affect my life. But ignoring it didn’t stop my COPD from making itself known. Shortness of breath was really impacting my day to day.”

With support and clinical intervention, Mark was able to better manage his COPD and get back to doing more of the things he loves. Now, he wants others living with COPD to know help is available to manage their condition.

COPD IS A complex and progressive disease that can make breathing more difficult over time.

COPD can be caused by inflammation in the airways that causes damage to parts of your lungs. Patients with COPD may also have chronic bronchitis and/or emphysema.

People with COPD can experience persistent cough, excessive mucus production, wheezing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath. Understanding COPD is important, and recognizing when the disease may not be adequately controlled is critical. Living with uncertainty around flare-ups can carry an emotional weight as well, says Corinne Young, nurse practitioner, pulmonary disease specialist, who is the Founder/Executive Director of the Association of Pulmonary Advanced Practice Providers.

Flare-ups, also known as exacerbations, are the worsening of COPD symptoms over several days. They can happen to anyone with COPD. During a flare-up, difficulty breathing, wheezing, and coughing can intensify and take longer to resolve. Even one flare-up can lead to permanent lung damage.

Young, who in addition to seeing patients, competes in team roping at rodeos, knows the importance of paying attention to changing conditions—a perspective she brings to helping patients recognize when their COPD may be inadequately controlled.

“The biggest predictor of a flare-up is a previous flare-up, and they start to get closer and closer together,” Young explains. For example, someone may experience a flare-up or exacerbation once every two years, then once a year, then every six months, then every three. “Inflammatory responses in the body drive these exacerbations, and that may lower lung function,” Young adds. That decline can increase the risk of additional flare-ups, perpetuating the cycle.

AS MARK’S COPD became more difficult to manage, it increasingly interfered with the life he was used to living. Shortness of breath and frequent flare-ups made it harder to work, travel, and do as many of the things he enjoyed. Eventually, he made the difficult decision to retire early from his job as a field service engineer.

Even after stepping away from work, Mark continued to struggle with his COPD. “I remember feeling like, ‘Well, I guess this is my life now,’” he says.

IN THE FALL of 2024, Mark underwent a pulmonary function test, bracing for bad news. The results confirmed that his current treatment plan was no longer adequately managing his COPD, prompting a discussion with his pulmonologist about what to do next. His doctor explained that Mark’s high eosinophil count could be a sign of type 2 inflammation. With this information, Mark and his doctor explored other treatment options, including Dupixent® (dupilumab).

Dupixent is a prescription medicine used with other medicines for the maintenance treatment of adults with inadequately controlled COPD and a high number of blood eosinophils (a type of white blood cell that may contribute to your COPD). Dupixent is used to reduce the number of flare-ups and can improve your breathing.

Dupixent is not used to relieve sudden breathing problems and will not replace an inhaled rescue medicine.

Do not use if you are allergic to dupilumab or to any of the ingredients in Dupixent.

Dupixent can cause serious side effects, such as allergic reactions, including skin reactions, that can sometimes be severe, eye problems, and joint aches and pain.

Please see additional Important Safety Information below.

Mark noticed a difference after adding Dupixent. “I could breathe better,” he says. Now, Mark feels less winded, and he’s doing more of the things he loves. “I’m really grateful that I can enjoy my hobbies more without constantly thinking about my COPD,” he adds.

For Mark, better breathing started with an honest conversation. Young encourages anyone living with COPD to be open with their healthcare provider, who can explain the full range of treatment options available. “It’s not just inhalers anymore—there are a lot of options,” she says.

Like bull riders who stay alert to changing conditions, people living with COPD can watch for signs that their disease may be inadequately controlled and talk with their doctor about their treatment options. With the right support, they may be able to enjoy more of the moments that matter to them—including, for some, time spent in the rodeo stands.

IMPORTANT SAFETY INFORMATION & INDICATION

Dupixent is a prescription medicine used with other medicines for the maintenance treatment of adults with inadequately controlled COPD and a high number of blood eosinophils (a type of white blood cell that may contribute to your COPD). Dupixent is used to reduce the number of flare-ups and can improve your breathing.

Do not use if you are allergic to dupilumab or to any of the ingredients in DUPIXENT®.

Before using DUPIXENT, tell your healthcare provider about all your medical conditions, including if you:

Tell your healthcare provider about all the medicines you take, including prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal supplements.

Especially tell your healthcare provider if you are taking oral, topical, or inhaled corticosteroid medicines or have COPD and also have asthma. Do not change or stop your other medicines, including corticosteroid medicine or other asthma medicine, without talking to your healthcare provider. This may cause other symptoms that were controlled by those medicines to come back.

DUPIXENT can cause serious side effects, including:

The most common side effects in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease include injection site reactions, common cold symptoms (nasopharyngitis), high count of a certain white blood cell (eosinophilia), viral infection, back pain, inflammation inside the nose (rhinitis), diarrhea, stomach problems (gastritis), joint pain (arthralgia), toothache, headache, and urinary tract infection.

Tell your healthcare provider if you have any side effect that bothers you or that does not go away. These are not all the possible side effects of DUPIXENT. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You are encouraged to report negative side effects of prescription drugs to the FDA. Visit www.fda.gov/medwatch, or call 1-800-FDA-1088.

Use DUPIXENT exactly as prescribed by your healthcare provider. It’s an injection given under the skin (subcutaneous injection). Your healthcare provider will decide if you or your caregiver can inject DUPIXENT. Do not try to prepare and inject DUPIXENT until you or your caregiver have been trained by your healthcare provider.

Please see accompanying full Prescribing Information including Patient Information.

Learn more about Dupixent at Dupixent.com/COPD.

DUPIXENT is a registered trademark of Sanofi or an affiliate.

#4729. RFK Jr.’s Revised Vaccine Schedule May Cause 83% Surge in Hepatitis B Infections

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s proposed changes to the childhood vaccine schedule have raised alarm among public health experts and researchers.

Concerns include a rise in preventable infectious diseases such as measles, polio, and hepatitis B.

A new study suggests that delaying or foregoing the hepatitis B shot for newborns could increase chronic infections among children.

In December 2025, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) ended its recommendation for universal hepatitis B vaccination at birth for infants whose mothers test negative for the virus. Instead, the federal health agency recommends individual-based clinical decision making.

After reviewing the evidence, the CDC, which is overseen by the HHS, concluded that newborns “face little risk of contracting hepatitis,” which deemed the vaccine, typically administered at birth, unnecessary.

Experts say this shift in public health policy wasn’t based on science, and researchers warn of rising infection rates.

“Hepatitis B immunizations have been proven to protect individuals against a serious and significant disease,” said Graham Tse, MD, pediatrician and chief medical officer of MemorialCare Miller Children’s & Women’s Hospital in Long Beach, CA.

“The hepatitis B vaccines have several decades of history and have been proven safe and effective,” Tse said. “There has been no new data or evidence presented or uncovered to support delaying the newborn dose of hepatitis B.”

Here’s what parents should know about making informed decisions with their child’s healthcare team.

A U.S. modeling study published in Annals of Internal Medicine on October 20 projected that delaying the first vaccine dose until 2 months could increase chronic hepatitis B infections among infants by 19% under one scenario.

With shared decision making and lower vaccine uptake, projected increases ranged from 83% to 225%, compared with universal birth-dose vaccination.

The researchers also estimated that up to 1.8 million young adults could remain susceptible to hepatitis B by age 20 under shared decision making, compared with 232,000 under universal birth dosing.

Another study published in JAMA Pediatrics in late April projected hundreds of additional chronic infections annually if the hepatitis B birth dose were delayed or omitted.

However, these figures are model-based projections, rather than verified outcomes. Actual results will depend on vaccination rates and other factors.

In December 2025, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) adopted a recommendation shifting away from universal hepatitis B vaccination at birth for infants whose mothers test negative for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg).

Under the new approach, parents and healthcare professionals can decide together whether to give the first dose at birth or defer it until the baby is 2 months old.

The change followed an 8 to 3 vote by the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), marking a departure from longstanding U.S. guidance.

However, infants born to mothers who test positive for hepatitis B or whose infection status is unknown should still receive the hepatitis B vaccine and hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) within 12 hours of birth, according to the updated guidelines.

Hepatitis B is a viral infection that affects the liver.

Although some infections resolve, newborns and infants face a higher risk of developing lifelong hepatitis B infection compared with adults.

Up to 90% of infants infected during their first year develop chronic hepatitis B.

“We have actual world evidence that vaccinating newborns for hepatitis B prevents hepatitis B infections later in life and the serious complications of that disease,” Tse said.

Over time, chronic infection can lead to cirrhosis, liver failure, or liver cancer.

“The danger of delaying the newborn hepatitis B shot is that individuals do not get vaccinated and thereby do not have protection against hepatitis B,” Tse said.

Early vaccination helps protect young infants before potential exposure occurs, including situations in which maternal screening misses an infection.

“Newborns can be infected with hepatitis B from a mother who is not aware they have a hepatitis B infection or from exposure later in life,” Tse said.

“The risk is developing a hepatitis B infection, which can potentially lead to liver cancer, fulminant hepatitis, or severe end-stage liver disease.”

In contrast to the CDC, the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) still recommends a universal hepatitis B vaccine dose within 24 hours of birth, followed by additional doses during infancy.

The leading pediatric medical organization has raised concerns about the potential consequences of reduced vaccination rates.

The hepatitis B vaccine has decades of safety and effectiveness data.

Tse said the AAP’s vaccine schedule and recommendations are based on decades of study, use, and expert input, and provide the best protection against vaccine-preventable diseases.

Parents who have questions about potential side effects, timing, or their baby’s individual risk should discuss them with a qualified healthcare professional.

“Parents are confused, given the recommendations from CDC, HHS, and Kennedy differ from established and respected groups such as the American Academy of Pediatrics, the Infectious Disease Society of America, and several states,” Tse said.

“Parents desire to keep their children safe, and having differing opinions and confusion will lead to reduced vaccination rates as parents experience doubt as to whom to listen to or believe.”

While the updated CDC policy offers more flexibility for some families, lower vaccination uptake could lead to an increase in chronic hepatitis B infections.

Ask your pediatrician about the benefits of vaccination against hepatitis B at birth, the risks of delaying the first dose, and the recommended schedule for completing the series.

You can also ask how maternal screening results affect your baby’s protection.

An informed conversation with your healthcare professional can help you weigh the evidence and choose a vaccination plan for your baby.

“I see no argument whatsoever for changing the established vaccination schedule for hepatitis B,” Tse said.

“There have been no new studies, no data, nor evidence to justify Kennedy’s proposed changes to the childhood immunization schedule. Delaying vaccinations or skipping vaccinations puts your child at risk for serious and significant diseases, which are all preventable,” Tse said.
