#4713. Letter from the Editor-in-Chief: The Good and the Hard of Life on GLP-1s

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

“Years of diets that worked for a couple of months, then gave all the weight back and more. Now the food noise has gone quiet,” a GLP-1 user shared.

In June, our brilliant News team published a piece about actor Mayim Bialik and her challenging experience with GLP-1 side effects. It did well, like many of the celebrity + health condition + human-interest angle features we create tend to do with our audience (that’s you all reading this!). Not a massive viral hit by any measure, but a strong performer on the traffic front.

Jump forward nearly 4 months; our equally brilliant social media team posts the piece on Facebook, leading with one of Bialik’s quotes from the article: “GLP-1s have helped people in serious need. Of that I am certain. But nobody talks much about what happens when it goes wrong.”

The fuse was lit. Nearly 12k likes, 1k reposts, and 3.5k comments later, the team had their most engaged post of the year by some margin. The irony is not lost on me that Bialik’s quote, about how rarely people talk about side effects, sparked such a deep conversation about that very thing.

GLP-1s are a big topic for Healthline. They drive traffic, they drive revenue, and they offer a rich seam of human-centric storytelling for our teams. Even so, no one predicted the post would catch fire the way it did. Our social team’s read is that a few things stacked up: Mayim Bialik is a name our Facebook audience knows, the topic is one where nearly everyone has a stake, and a busy thread tends to get shown to more people, who then add more comments. That’s the hypothesis. What we’ve consistently seen is that posts that lead with a quote get more people talking than those that lead with a headline. You may have noticed this article takes the same approach.

We also know that the comment sections on social media aren’t always the most hospitable of environments, particularly in the health space. What stood out about the lion’s share of the comments we read was how constructive the discourse was. People were leading with deeply personal and often moving perspectives about the life changing impact (for good and bad) of GLP-1s. In turn, they were met with equally balanced and thoughtful responses.

Many of the comments expanded on Bialik’s experience, detailing long and difficult battles with a range of side effects. But plenty told the other side of the story: years of failed diets and struggles with chronic conditions leading to despondency, side effects that went on to ease with time, and life changing results that were ultimately worth the cost.

The line that opened this piece could have come from any of those commenters. It didn’t. It came from Kitty Hough, who is 75 and lives in London. Eagle-eyed readers will have spotted that she has the same surname as me – that’s because she’s my mom. She’s one of two people closer to the Healthline home who spoke to me for this piece and whose stories echo the Facebook post thread, with the good and the hard bits side by side.

Kitty was a hockey player and distance runner as a girl, the kind who could eat what she liked without it showing. Then came children, and a weight that crept up year after year, with decades of diets that “worked for a couple of months only to be back to my former weight and then some.” In late 2024, after a lot of research, she decided to try tirzepatide.

Since then, Kitty has lost 56 pounds. She says her joints hurt less, which she puts down to reduced inflammation. She is more mobile. The constant chatter about food has faded. She thinks harder before she eats now.

“I am a strong believer that obesity is a disease and in my case certainly not the result of overindulgence or laziness,” she says. “GLP-1s have greatly improved my health and self-esteem. After years of struggling with my weight, I have finally found a way to solve the problem.”

Kitty will also tell you what it cost. Nausea. Constipation. Sulfur-tasting burps and rough nights of indigestion. Initial hair loss that has since grown back, and loose skin. Muscle loss. And she misses some of the true joy of cooking and eating food.

But despite bumps in her journey, Kitty remains convinced that the benefits of GLP-1s for her life and health outweigh any drawbacks she’s experienced. “I am conscious that I will probably be on this drug for a long time if not for life. It is truly a miracle drug.”

I also spoke to Ann Marie Maguire, AGNP-C, RN, TCTCN, a nurse practitioner specializing in transplantation and cellular therapy, the sister of Healthline’s Chief Business Officer Christine Macguire, and someone who has lost over 50lbs since starting GLP-1s in 2022.

“I struggled with my weight since my teens and always believed I should be able to manage it on my own. But in my 30s, my knees were hurting just getting out of bed or walking to dinner. I realized how much my weight was affecting my quality of life. Starting a GLP-1 in 2022, alongside healthier eating and exercise, made a tremendous difference. My only regret is not starting sooner,” said Ann Marie.

As a healthcare professional, Ann Marie also identified cost as a major factor that can’t be ignored regarding GLP-1s and their impact.

“There’s understandable debate about the long-term use and cost of these medications,” she says. “But we also need to consider the health and financial burden of obesity, including cardiovascular complications, hospitalizations, surgeries and ongoing medications. The cost conversation should account for the potential benefits of preventing or reducing those complications.”

Ann Marie points to a frustration many patients will recognize: reaching a healthier weight can become the reason coverage gets cut off. “We don’t automatically stop blood pressure medication because a patient’s readings improve,” she says. The treatment may be what’s keeping the condition controlled. Obesity, she argues, deserves the same approach. “Reaching a goal weight can mean treatment is working, and decisions about continuing it should reflect the patient’s ongoing needs, benefits and side effects.”

It’s important to note that this article looks at the experiences of only a handful of people out of the millions who now take GLP-1s. Like all drugs, these medications are not right for everyone. Side effects are common; some of them can be serious, and both the long-term impact and what happens when people stop are still being worked out. Ultimately, your care team, with knowledge of your medical history, is a far better guide than a comment thread.

Yet the evidence now reaches well beyond the scales: large trials have linked semaglutide to fewer heart attacks and strokes in people with heart disease and slower kidney decline in people with diabetes and kidney disease, and tirzepatide became the first FDA-approved drug for moderate to severe sleep apnea in adults with obesity.

Stories like Kitty’s, Ann Marie’s, Mayim Bialik’s, and those of the 3.5k commenters on the Facebook post aren’t proof of what will happen to you one way or another. But for a lot of people, my mom included, these drugs have changed what an ordinary day looks like, and in many cases changed what their future can look like.

One of the most significant drug developments of the century so far? Hard to argue with.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Wednesday in our Healthline Wellness Wire newsletter.

#4712. Tesla launches Robotaxi in San Antonio with a 274 sq mi geofence on paper

Tesla is launching its Robotaxi service in San Antonio, its eighth city, with a launch geofence covering about 274 square miles. That’s the biggest day-one map Tesla has ever posted, and more than four times the size of Waymo’s San Antonio service area.

But if Tesla’s recent maps are any guide, a big chunk of that area won’t be bookable. In Austin, an independent check found the Robotaxi app only accepted pickups and drop-offs in about 59% of the zone Tesla advertises.

Tesla’s official Robotaxi account made the announcement just after midnight local time: “Robotaxi available in San Antonio starting tomorrow, 5am.” It came with a map of the “launch geofence,” a large polygon that runs from Loop 1604 on the north side down to just south of downtown.

Robotaxi Tracker, which measures operator maps and logs fleet sightings, puts the zone at 274 square miles. That covers about 1.0 million residents (51% of the metro) and 721,000 jobs. San Antonio International Airport sits inside the polygon, but it isn’t served.

Waymo started driverless rides in San Antonio in February with more than 60 square miles and opened to all riders in October, airport trips included. Robotaxi Tracker currently lists Waymo’s San Antonio area at 59 square miles.

What Tesla didn’t say is how many cars will cover its 274 square miles. As of Monday morning, Robotaxi Tracker hadn’t logged a single Tesla Robotaxi in San Antonio.

The launch landed the same day Tesla expanded Austin again. The tracker now measures Tesla’s Austin zone at 443 square miles, up 178 square miles since mid-September.

We’ve seen this movie. Last month, Tesla expanded its Houston geofence into the shape of a rocket, and within two days the creator of Robotaxi Tracker found the app refusing downtown pickups inside it.

Since then, Koby Pierce, who tracks Tesla’s service on X, has done the tedious work of checking city after city. He searched thousands of real addresses in the Robotaxi app on an emulator and mapped only the ones where Tesla allows a pickup or drop-off, then compared that with the map Tesla advertises. Here’s the share of Tesla’s advertised land area that actually works:

Austin's dropoff/pickup Geofence is ~41% smaller than advertised.Seems mostly the East side of town is inaccessible. Unsure the cause. Any ideas?Dallas is next and should be done by noon tomrrow. pic.twitter.com/WvU99sJlJh

Austin is the one that matters. It’s Tesla’s flagship market, with 453 unsupervised vehicles in service according to Robotaxi Tracker. Yet about 41% of the advertised map Pierce tested, mostly on the east side of town, wouldn’t take a ride request. Pierce points to railroad crossings as a big factor in several cities, which lines up with the strange downtown routing we saw in Houston.

To be fair, Pierce says Waymo is next on his list, and he expects “they’re no better.” Robotaxi Tracker already had to trim Waymo’s Orlando area last month after finding the airport, inside Waymo’s published map, wasn’t selectable. We’ll look at those numbers when they’re out. But it doesn’t change what Tesla is doing with San Antonio today.

Credit where it’s due. A 274-square-mile launch in a new city is progress, and Tesla now runs unsupervised rides in eight cities. At the start of this year, it had no unsupervised rides anywhere.

But we need to stop taking Tesla’s geofence numbers at face value, and that includes us. We used Tesla’s 254-square-mile figure for Houston, and it turned out to be overstated. In all six cities Pierce has checked, the real service area is between 59% and 78% of what Tesla posts. In Austin and Miami, it’s about 60%.

So the honest way to read the San Antonio announcement is “up to 274 square miles.” In practice, expect something closer to 160 to 210 square miles, with an unknown number of cars, and the airport already off the table. That’s still bigger than Waymo’s 59 square miles in the city.

These maps are mostly fiction. I live inside the Houston map but the app says I am outside. If you drive to where the app allows, no vehicles are ever available. Waymos are a routine site and are available on a short notice. This is smoke and mirrors to shore up the company value ahead of the SpaceX merger.

The problem is that square miles are the metric Tesla fully controls. Drawing a polygon costs nothing, and the numbers were all over X within hours of the post. Cars per square mile, wait times, and rides completed are much harder to inflate, and nationally Waymo still runs over 4,000 driverless vehicles to Tesla’s 666, per Robotaxi Tracker.

I still consider this a small pilot by any standard, and safety remains the bottleneck. Tesla is still forcing riders through hour-long rides that should take 15 minutes because they have to take routes that avoid areas that Tesla can’t safely navigate without supervision.

Until that’s fixed, robotaxi won’t be able to meaningfully scale beyond these limited demonstrations in geo-fenced areas.

Robotaxi or not, most EV charging still happens at home, and pairing it with rooftop solar can cut your cost per mile to nearly zero. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. #4711. Why Better Recovery Might Be the Missing Link in Your Workout Routine

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

You work hard in the gym, nail your nutrition, and consistently try to challenge yourself with heavier weights or more reps. But no matter what you do lately, it seems as if your progress just won’t budge. So what’s going on?

A plateau can be incredibly frustrating, but there is some good news: It may not be your meticulously planned workouts that need tweaking. The solution for your stall in progress may lie in something a little simpler: recovery.

Many people think results happen during our sweat sessions, but in actuality, the gains we’re working toward happen afterward. Adapting to stress, building muscle, and getting stronger all happen when we take rest. So, before you fire your personal trainer or scour the internet for a new workout plan, try making a few simple tweaks to how you spend your downtime, if you’re even giving yourself any.

Read on for what the science and experts say about recovery—and how you can use yours to escape your fitness plateau.

Meet the experts: Donna Duffy, PhD, is an associate professor in the department of kinesiology at the University of North Carolina, Greensboro, and head of research at Collective X Health, a women's health intelligence and research platform co-founded by WH advisory board member Stacy Sims. Lisa Woodroffe, MD, is a sports medicine physician at the University of Iowa Health Care and team doctor for several of the Iowa Hawkeye women’s athletic teams. Asad Siddiqi, DO, is the chief of rehabilitation medicine at NewYork-Presbyterian Brooklyn Methodist Hospital.

Working out is only one piece of the equation when it comes to seeing results. In order to get all the benefits of training, your body needs time to rest and recover after a workout. “During rest, your body recovers using sleep, food, and downtime to repair the tissues you’ve stressed during training and prepare them to handle the next challenge,” says Donna Duffy, PhD, an associate professor in the department of kinesiology at the University of North Carolina, Greensboro.

There’s a lot that goes on in your body during rest: In addition to your muscles repairing and building back stronger, you experience a nervous system reset—as your heart rate decreases after a training session, your body shifts out of a stressed state and begins to calm down, Duffy explains. Then there is increased blood flow during and after exercise, which helps flush out things like lactic acid and delivers fresh oxygen and nutrients to stressed parts of the body.

That is, assuming you’re giving your body enough time to do all that. “If you continually pile more workouts on top of fatigue without giving your body enough time and resources to recover, that fatigue can start to interfere with your overall performance in and out of the gym,” Duffy says.

When a person fails to recover adequately, a weight that seemed doable on Monday feels heavier on Wednesday, and an easy run becomes a hard one. All of this can be incredibly frustrating, and may make people think they just need to work harder, but experts say sometimes the opposite is true. “Your body may not need more training,” says Duffy. “Instead, it may need more opportunity to recover from the training you're already doing.”

Your body may be sending you signals that you’re not as well recovered as you think. According to Duffy, some common signs that your body has not recovered well include:

Showing signs of poor recovery? Start by making these tweaks.

When deciding if your body needs a rest, consider factors like workout duration, intensity, and fatigue, says Asad Siddiqi, DO, chief of rehabilitation medicine at NewYork-Presbyterian Brooklyn Methodist Hospital. Soreness or fatigue that stays below a 3 to 4 out of 10 during or immediately after training and does not last beyond 24 to 36 hours is the upper limit of “acceptable” exercise-induced discomfort, and a day in between loading is probably fine. Meanwhile, if you go above a 5, Dr. Siddiqi recommends taking an extra day beyond that to monitor how you’re recovering before doing the same workout again. Typically, a two-day break will allow people enough time to recover, but the most important barometer is how you feel, he says. If you’re still super sore and think your form will be compromised, you need more time off.

Bob and Brad A7 Pro Massage Gun with Heat and Cold Therapy

TriggerPoint Grid Multi-Density Foam Roller

This doesn’t mean you need to be completely inactive during those days off, particularly if you’re doing circuit training. If you hit arms really hard on Monday and need to give them some extra time to recover, you can still do legs the next day. But, if you are doing intense and fatiguing full-body workouts, try alternating resistance training with low-impact aerobic or mobility exercises like yoga.

Even if you’re doing circuit training, at a minimum, most people should have at least one full rest day per week, says Lisa Woodroffe, MD, a sports medicine physician at the University of Iowa Health Care and team doctor for several of the Iowa Hawkeye women’s athletic teams. And, if you’re someone who has been feeling consistently sore, unusually fatigued, or seeing a dip in performance, it’s time to up your number of rest days.

For a variety of reasons, many active people are just simply not eating enough, says Dr. Woodroffe. “They are either underestimating how much energy they are expending in exercise, or overestimating what they are eating, or with busy schedules running out of time in their day to get everything they need.” It’s also worth mentioning that some people may be exercising with the explicit goal of losing weight—which can result in underfueling for their workouts, she says.

Eating enough is critical for recovery. “We know that insufficient fueling patterns have cascading and multiplying effects on the body’s ability to respond to training load and recovery,” Dr. Woodroffe says. “All cells of the body need adequate energy to maintain optimal function. When there is not enough energy to go around, there will be effects not only at the cellular level but eventually also at the organ system level.” We’re talking effects on muscle recovery, bone density, cardiovascular function, and cognitive performance.

That’s why experts recommend having a plan in place for getting all the fuel you need. “Emphasizing a routine of three to five meals a day that includes carbs for energy, protein for muscle building, and fresh vegetables and fruits for minerals and gut health is the baseline,” says Dr. Siddiqi. You don’t need to count calories if that’s not your thing—but you should have a goal of at least three meals supplemented by additional snacks every day that hit all of the macros (carbs, protein, and fats).

Protein is particularly important for active people, but no macro should be ignored. Dr. Woodroffe always notes that no food groups should be restricted unless otherwise directed by a medical professional. If you need any help with your fueling strategy, it’s a good idea to check in with a doctor or dietitian who can give you personalized recommendations.

One overall, simple way to make sure you’re eating enough? Feeling full. You should eat to be satiated and not feel constantly hungry. When it comes to snacking, it’s recommended that you eat easily digestible carbs (Think: fruit, bagels, toast) 30 to 60 minutes before a workout, and then a combination of carbs, protein, and fluids within 60 minutes following. It’s one reason dietitians love chocolate milk as a post-workout drink.

Your training program is a balancing act. “A plateau can happen either due to not enough training, or not enough recovery,” Dr. Woodroffe says. But how can we actually tell which one is happening? What are the clues that someone needs to pull back versus increase the challenge?

“Overall, training should be a positive experience that challenges the body and mind but doesn’t put you out of commission,” Dr. Siddiqi says. You want to be sore after a workout, but not so much that you can’t move. If you’re experiencing the symptoms above that are signs you’re not recovering properly, you’re probably overloading and should pull back. Start by taking two full rest days to give your body a real chance to recover, and then consider implementing one additional rest day per week compared to your old schedule or adjusting your training plan to allow for less intensity.

On the flip side, if you’re plateauing and not feeling drained at all, then it may be because you need to challenge yourself more. If that’s the case, Dr. Siddiqi recommends a steady increase in load by roughly 10 percent week over week. “The definition of ‘load’ in this situation is variable, and so this could mean 10 percent more intense based on your perceived exertion, 10 percent greater distance, 10 percent greater duration, or however else you think could be meaningful,” he says. The key, though, is to have a steady increase on your way to your goal, avoiding any major spikes.

So how do you know when symptoms are more than just poor recovery after a challenging workout versus a health issue that needs a professional follow-up? “Sometimes fatigue, soreness, or a dip in performance really can be a sign that you need more recovery, but it's also important not to assume that every change is caused by your training,” says Duffy. “If symptoms are persistent, getting worse, or affecting your ability to function normally, there may be something else going on.”

Duffy suggests seeing a health care professional if:

Whatever you may be experiencing—a regular old case of doing too much or something more serious—consider this your sign to take a second, check in with yourself, and don’t hesitate to ask for support. You’ll be out there moving again (and even better) before you know it.

#4710. The Best Winter Jackets for Men, Tested by Style Editors

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

We tried more than 40 options to find the ones worth wearing all season.

MEN’S HEALTH EDITORS spend a lot of time outdoors. We commute to our NYC office, then juggle the gym, errands, and weekend outings. So when cold weather hits, we need winter coats that can get us through nearly every icy scenario imaginable. Gone are the days when staying warm meant looking like a walking snowman. Today’s outerwear pairs advanced insulation with weather-resistant fabrics and thoughtful details to help keep you warm when the temperatures drop. The best designs layer comfortably, move well, and still look sharp.

As someone who tests gear year-round—and as part of a team that’s been reviewing winter coats since 2019—I’ve worn everything from lightweight puffers on frosty commutes to parkas in sub-zero conditions. Along the way, the Men’s Health style team has put more than 40 coats through real-life use: daily city commutes, snowy trail days, and ski trips. We look at how warm they actually feel, how well they move, how tough the materials are, and whether they look good off the rack. And after all that, Mack Weldon, Columbia, and Canada Goose rose to the top as the best winter coats for men.

I’ve been getting my wear out of Mack Weldon’s WarmKnit Air Hooded Jacket for the past year and it surprised me with its performance. At first glance, you’d think it’s just a lightweight puffer built for those mild 50- to 60-degree temps. But I found it could hang in the 40s, too—and still keep me warm. That’s thanks to its Thinsulate fill, synthetic insulation made of ultra-fine fibers, which does the heavy lifting without making me feel like a bloated marshmallow. It’s water- and wind-resistant, so a little drizzle or gusty wind doesn’t ruin a commute either.

The snap-button front and the two-way zipper make it easy to get in and out of, and the structured hood actually stays put, protecting your head without flopping around or blowing off. Just like most of Mack Weldon’s winter collection, sporty casual meets performance is the vibe here, so you can wear it with anything from a sweatsuit to a casual crewneck over chinos. With bonded quilting and interior pockets, it's both functional and polished, so it works for weekend hikes or casual dinners.

That said, there are trade‑offs. The jacket’s waist‑length cut means it won’t cover your core the way a mid‑thigh parka does, so in truly cold winter conditions you’ll feel more exposed around hips and lower back. If you need serious warmth for winter storms, opt for a longer cut; if you want a versatile everyday coat for mild to moderately cold weather, this is a standout value pick.

For days when you want warmth without the bulk, this Columbia down jacket delivers in spades. It uses Omni‑Heat reflective lining—those tiny silver dots that bounce your body heat back at you—which helps keep heat where you want it even as temperatures dip and winds pick up. It’s the kind of jacket you reach for when you want to feel cozy without feeling weighed down.

The 650‑fill down has enough loft to stay warm without ballooning your silhouette, and the baffle construction keeps insulation evenly distributed while creating a streamlined look that’s more polished than many puffers of similar warmth. Columbia also packs in tech‑forward features like HeatSeal construction to trap warmth while still allowing breathability and Omni‑Shield for moisture resistance and stain repellency—handy when you’re trudging through slush or, as I once did, surviving a spilled coffee on the way to the bus.

What I appreciate most is how easily it layers: It slips over a fleece or hoodie without feeling stiff, and it’s comfortable enough to wear all day whether you’re heading to work or exploring snowy trails. It’s not the warmest jacket around, but for everyday winter conditions where you want mobility and comfort with insulation, it’s a fantastic pick.

This is, quite simply, one of the best budget winter jackets we’ve tested—and it’s worth your attention even if you usually steer clear of ultra‑affordable picks. Deals and Trends Editor Tim Kohut wore the coat zipped up, and found that the heavyweight insulation did a solid job at keeping the shivers at bay on a brisk walk to the train — all without overheating once he hit the warm subway platform.

The polyester shell is water-repellent, not waterproof, so he can survive light showers without them soaking through to his clothes. It may not be the best option for heavy rain, so if you’re staring down a prolonged rainstorm, an umbrella or rain layer is still a smart call. Its relaxed fit is roomy enough for you to fit a chunky sweater underneath without bulk. Kohut rocked a T-shirt and chunky cardigan, and did not feel like the Michelin Man after being fully zipped up. The hood doesn’t cinch tight — one of the few real drawbacks — which lets cold air sneak in on windier days, but it is fleece‑lined for extra comfort and warmth.

Pockets are straightforward but functional, and the simple styling means this jacket works for daily commuting as easily as casual weekends. For the price, it’s a total win if you want something warm, reliable, and unfussy without dropping big cash.

Our Grooming Editor Sean Zucker wore this parka in every cold-weather situation: long commutes, chilly hikes, snowball fights. It has a slim puffer design but with a longer cut and more down, making it warmer for bone-chilling morning walks to the coffee shop. Zucker recently got caught in a sudden downpour, and the waterproof—not just water-resistant—shell kept him completely dry. On a freezing 30-degree cold and windy day, he stayed warm and comfortable the entire time. Plus, the storm cuffs blocked icy gusts from sneaking in at the sleeves.

He also appreciated the two-way zipper, which you don’t see on a lot of winter coats. It made hopping on and off the subway or sitting at a café easy without feeling restricted. While the insulated hood isn’t super spacious, it cinches close enough to trap heat. The fit is stylish without feeling bulky, and his hands fit perfectly in the pockets—small detail, but it really makes a difference when it’s freezing out. Yes, it’s an investment piece, but with premium 700-fill down warmth, waterproof and windproof protection, and thoughtful features, this parka is a true workhorse built to handle harsh conditions.

Canada Goose’s coat may come with some sticker shock, but our Style and Reviews Director Christian Gollayan has made good use of it for the past three winters. He wears it to walk his two corgis, and between the snow, wind, and icy sidewalks, it keeps him warm without feeling like he’s lugging around a heavy sleeping bag. The Arctic Tech fabric—a polyester-cotton blend—has structure without stiffness, so it handles those brutal days when the wind tries to cut straight through you. Its longer silhouette offers extra coverage in snowy conditions. Not to mention, it’s a stylish coat, so you’re getting warmth and thoughtful design versus a bulky, shapeless puffer.

Like Fjallraven’s parka, this one has more pockets than your average coat—four outside, three inside. Two are great for thawing frozen mitts, and the others have flaps that help secure smaller essentials like a wallet, beanie, or winter gloves. There’s even a down-filled hood that feels toasty without making you feel stuffy, plus backpack-style straps if you want to carry it hands-free while running errands or grabbing coffee.

Sure, it’s very pricey, but we had to bite the bullet and think about the bigger picture. Stepping outside doesn’t feel like wrestling with the elements anymore. Between warmth, thoughtful design, and sleek style, it’s become our go-to armor for extreme weather—and it’s already survived three ruthless winter seasons in a row.

Men’s Health designer Jason Speakman took this burly parka from Fjallraven out on the slopes during a trip to Aspen. At 6 feet tall with a slender build, he found that this jacket wasn’t suffocating or too heavy, letting him flex, bend, and twist easily while carving turns or easing down steep trails. The fleece-lined hood with detachable faux fur edging kept his head and ears warm on icy chairlift rides, and he could easily remove the fur for a sleeker après-ski look. Thanks to the drawcords at the neck, it pulls tight around your face to shut out breezes.

This coat has eight pockets—more than any on the list—including roomy zippered chest pockets that fit slim essentials like a phone or cardholder. Its weight-to-warmth ratio is excellent; after five hours on the snow, Speakman stayed warm without feeling like he was wearing a stiff, overstuffed parka. The fit is generous, allowing space to pile base layers and still keep a clean profile.

Down and synthetic insulation are two of the most common options.

Synthetic insulation is made from polyester fibers, more affordable than down, and handles wet weather better. Popular options include PrimaLoft and Thinsulate, which use a blend of synthetic fibers designed to trap heat while remaining lightweight and breathable.

Down is made from clusters of goose or duck plumage, and is prized for its lightweight warmth. It compresses easily for packing and offers superior heat retention in dry conditions. Some coats even blend down and synthetic fill to combine the benefits of both.

Look for a waterproof shell, sealed seams, and a protective hood to help keep rain and snow from soaking through. Features like adjustable cuffs and storm flaps can also help block out wind and moisture. If you’re dealing with wet, snowy winters, prioritize a fully waterproof design over a water-resistant finish.

A winter coat should leave enough room to layer a sweater or hoodie without feeling bulky or restricting movement. The shoulders should sit comfortably, the sleeves should cover the wrists, and the hem should provide enough coverage for your needs. If you plan to wear it over heavier layers, consider sizing up, but always check the brand’s fit recommendations.

Look for fleece-lined hand pockets to keep your fingers warm and interior pockets to protect your phone, wallet, or AirPods from the cold. Extra details like zippered or hidden pockets add practicality, especially for commuting, travel, or outdoor adventures.

Our fashion team, led by Style and Reviews Director Christian Gollayan, tested more than 40 winter coats in real-world conditions, from freezing city commutes to snowy hikes, ski trips, and travel days spent shuffling between cold-weather airports. If a coat claimed to handle winter, we made sure it proved it. We focused on warmth, durability, fit, mobility, and practicality. We paid attention to how each coat insulated in different temperatures, whether the materials could stand up to wind and wet weather, how well the coat moved with us during long days out, and whether the design felt useful rather than overbuilt.

Details like pocket placement, zippers, adjustability, and overall comfort played a big role too. After months of wear and side-by-side comparisons, only the top performers made our final list. These are the winter coats that stayed warm, held up, and made our lives easier—not just in theory, but in brutal winter reality.

For most of us, the terms "jacket" and "coat" are probably interchangeable. However, the main difference comes down to length and coverage. A winter coat's main objective is to keep you warm, which is why it's bigger and thicker, extends past the hips or toward the knees, and is filled with some type of insulation. A jacket, on the other hand, is considered a combination of style and warmth. Jackets don't typically go past the waist and they're designed to be worn indoors at times. Winter jackets can be layered more with outfits too—sometimes even under a coat.

Winter jackets can work as your main outer layer in cold weather, especially when they’re insulated and long enough to provide adequate coverage. For colder temperatures or extended time outdoors, a longer, more heavily insulated coat or parka can provide additional warmth and protection. The right choice ultimately depends on the weather, your activity level, and how much you plan to layer underneath.

#4709. LiveWire just showed off its biggest electric motorcycle lineup yet

LiveWire has spent the last few years expanding beyond the premium electric motorcycles that originally defined the Harley-Davidson spin-off. But seeing the company’s latest machines all together at EICMA in Milan really drives home just how much broader LiveWire’s ambitions have become.

I stopped by the LiveWire booth at EICMA 2026, where the company had everything from its new lightweight S4 Honcho models to the freshly acquired DUST electric dirt bikes – plus STACYC’s electric balance bikes for the youngest riders.

It’s quite a spread, and perhaps more importantly, it paints a picture of a company that increasingly wants to have an electric two-wheeler for just about every stage of a rider’s life.

I also had a chance to spend several hours test-riding the S4 Honcho Street in Milan, so be on the lookout for that article and video to experience it with me.

But for now, let’s see what was at the LiveWire booth.

Perhaps the most important bikes at the booth were the S4 Honcho models, LiveWire’s new lightweight and lower-cost electric motorcycles.

The production S4 Honcho Street made its European debut at EICMA alongside the dirt-oriented S4 Honcho Trail. The Trail version recently began reaching customers in the US, with the Street now en route to dealerships, and European sales are beginning around the EICMA launch.

These bikes represent a significant departure from LiveWire’s earlier strategy. Instead of trying to compete directly with full-size gasoline motorcycles on outright performance, the Honcho platform is aimed at riders looking for something smaller, simpler, and more approachable.

And now the family is getting even bigger.

Also on display was the new S4 Honcho Skate, making its first public appearance.

The Skate is planned for 2027 and further expands the modular Honcho platform with a stripped-down, playful design.

For those who have followed H-D’s electric ambitions for as long as I have, you might even remember the original Harley-Davidson electric moped prototype that seems to have served as inspiration for the Honcho Skate’s design.

Seeing the various Honcho versions together also makes LiveWire’s strategy with the platform much clearer. Rather than creating one small electric motorcycle, the company is building an entire family around the concept.

The other major attraction at LiveWire’s booth was the DUST lineup.

LiveWire acquired the assets of DUST Moto earlier this year, bringing the lightweight electric dirt bike company under its umbrella. EICMA marked the first public showing of the production-intent DUST Hightail under LiveWire ownership.

The Hightail had already generated plenty of interest before the acquisition as a lightweight, high-performance electric dirt bike. Now we’re getting our first look at how that machine fits into LiveWire’s broader plans.

The company is targeting a 2027 introduction for the production Hightail.

LiveWire also showed the new DUST Spur, another model planned for 2027 and intended to expand the newly formed DUST family.

The DUST acquisition is particularly interesting because it gives LiveWire an immediate foothold in the rapidly growing lightweight electric off-road motorcycle space without having to develop an entirely new platform from scratch.

In what could be a hint at faster charging to come, there was an interesting S2 Alpanista Corsa motorcycle that had been outfitted with a NACS plug and DC fast-charging capabilities.

LiveWire claimed a 20-80% charge in under 10 minutes, which would revolutionize the ability to do long-distance motorcycle touring, or just make it more convenient to get a quick charge and head back to your apartment.

There’s on word on whether the concept will make it to production, but the specs are enticing!

The most interesting part of LiveWire’s EICMA display may not have been any individual motorcycle, but rather what happens when you stand back and look at the entire booth.

On one end you’ve got STACYC electric balance bikes. LiveWire says the brand has already introduced more than 250,000 riders to two wheels.

Then you’ve got the lightweight S4 Honcho family. Above that sit the DUST machines for more serious off-road riding, while LiveWire’s existing S2 motorcycles continue to cover the higher-performance street end of the spectrum.

That’s becoming something of an electric two-wheeler ladder.

A kid can theoretically start on a STACYC, graduate into increasingly capable electric two-wheelers, and eventually wind up on a proper electric motorcycle – all within the same corporate family.

And that feels particularly relevant at a show like EICMA, where much of the motorcycle industry is still trying to figure out exactly where electric motorcycles fit.

LiveWire seems increasingly convinced that the answer isn’t simply to build electric replacements for existing gasoline motorcycles.

Instead, the company is spreading out into categories where electric drivetrains can create different kinds of motorcycles altogether.

I’ve been following LiveWire’s evolution for years, and the company standing in front of me at EICMA looks considerably different from the one that started out selling a single expensive flagship electric motorcycle.

The big, high-performance bikes are still important, but machines like the S4 Honcho and DUST Hightail are arguably more interesting to me because they can bring entirely different riders into electric motorcycling.

They’re smaller. They’re simpler. And perhaps most importantly, they’re targeting the kind of fun, accessible riding that doesn’t require superbike levels of performance.

There’s still plenty we need to learn about several of these new models, particularly final specifications and pricing for the 2027 machines.

But seeing the Honcho, Honcho Skate, Hightail, Spur, and STACYC machines together at EICMA makes one thing pretty clear: LiveWire isn’t just trying to sell a few electric motorcycles anymore.

It’s trying to build an entire electric two-wheeler ecosystem.

#4708. A Renewed Humanism

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

Pope Leo’s Magnifica Humanitas (2026), subtitled “On Safeguarding the Human Person in the Time of Artificial Intelligence,” has been heralded as one of the most significant and morally serious visions for how humanity ought to think about and navigate the advent of the AI era. Acknowledging “the ambiguity of tools,” which are neither morally good nor bad in and of themselves but “can cause harm when not oriented toward the good,” the Pope insists that the end toward which our aspirations aim is as important as the aspirations themselves.

For Leo, protecting and fostering the dignity of the human person must be the goal of everything we do. Contrasting two images taken from Scripture, the Pope calls us to consider how the desire that orients our ambitions changes the things we create.

In Leo’s first example, the construction of the Tower of Babel (Genesis 11:1–9) is motivated by fear and vainglory:

Fearing being scattered across the earth, they [the builders] sought to guarantee stability and power for themselves, and above all to ‘make a name’ for themselves.” Such motives cannot but end in ruin. Leo continues, “When a city is built on pride and the claim to self-sufficiency, communication breaks down, languages are confused and people no longer understand each other. The result is not unity, but dispersion. Babel thus reveals the limits of any effort that, however grandiose, arises from self-affirmation, sacrifices human dignity for efficiency and aspires to reach heaven without God’s blessing.

In his second, which comes from the Book of Nehemiah, Nehemiah returns to the city of Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile only to find it in ruins. Heartbroken, he takes in the destruction in silence. Then, before setting to work, he “convened the families, assigned each of them a section of the wall to rebuild, listened to their concerns, coordinated their efforts and addressed any opposition.”

Nehemiah, that is, kept the dignity of those around him at the center of his project rather than running headlong toward apparent solutions. In so doing, he was able to resurrect what had been lost while simultaneously creating something new. The Pope writes:

The narrative shows how the city is reborn, not through the initiative of one man, but through the shared responsibility of all: men, women, priests, artisans, heads of households and young people all play a part. It is an undertaking with God at the center, which rebuilds relationships before rebuilding with stones. Thus, ancient Jerusalem rediscovers a common language—not one of uniformity, but one of communion, namely the harmony that arises when all persons assume their own role and recognize that their strength comes from the Lord.

What makes these images apt for our current moment—and what many commentators have overlooked—is the role language plays in each. For, if the desire of those constructing the Tower of Babel was to create a single, unified language with which all could understand and be understood, so too is the aim of Artificial Intelligence to provide a kind of totalizing language capable of flattening ambiguity and rendering difference obsolete. And if Nehemiah’s success was rooted in the fact that he sought out the input of those he hoped to serve, and even (perhaps especially) those with whom he disagreed, so too must dialogue be at the foundation of technological advance.

Consider another example, this one taken from contemporary fiction, that draws out this tension inherent in language—the tension between the desire to communicate directly, if only superficially, and the desire to express how fraught and complex human experience actually is, even if that expression can only be accomplished indirectly and ambiguously.

It comes from Paul Auster’s great work of metareal fiction City of Glass (1987), in which the story’s chief antagonist Peter Stillman—is he still a man, still human, or has he been deformed by his mad pursuit of “perfectibility”?—obsesses over the duplicity of language, the way one word can mean two equal and opposite things. For instance, the word cleave “means both ‘to join together’ and ‘to break apart.’”

For Stillman, the Genesis narrative to which the Pope alluded “records not only the fall of man, but the fall of language” from clarity to opacity. Once, he conjectures, language was simple, direct, and stated exactly what it meant to say without confusion or ambiguity. There was a time when “words had not been merely appended to things . . . they revealed their essences . . . A thing and its name were interchangeable.” But after the destruction of the Tower of Babel, this was no longer true. Now words conceal as much as they reveal, and deception is built into the very nature of how we communicate.

Driven mad by the desire to use language to reunify what appears to him to be a fractured and fragmentary existence, Stillman sets out to realize a utopian future in which his model of a single, unified language makes absolute knowledge and mastery possible. (Sound familiar?)

If the fall of man also entailed a fall of language, was it not logical to assume that it would be possible to undo the fall, to reverse its effects by undoing the fall of language? . . . If man could learn to speak this original language of innocence, did it not follow that he would thereby recover a state of innocence within himself?

The trouble is that Stillman is not able to conjure up this mythical language model, and his attempts to do so inflict immense suffering on those around him.

In an ironic twist, Stillman ultimately resorts to deception himself in a vain attempt to accomplish his goal. Creating a character named Henry Dark, a fictional disciple of John Milton, he attributes his most controversial ideas to Dark and even falsifies the historical record to make it appear as though Dark had heralded his, Stillman’s, project over 300 years in advance.

What could offer a better image of the LLMs that seem so powerful and omniscient today—with their false citations and hallucinated facts—than a fictional character invented by a mad genius to dupe others into believing that his language model could solve the mysteries and riddles of the human condition? And yet, what could offer a better reason to hope? For, although Dark was invented by Stillman to serve darker ends, still his creation was—as Pope Leo recently called the craft of writing fiction—a profound “act of humanity,” one which points to the supreme dignity of its author even if he, like many of us today, is too consumed with his utopian ideas to appreciate it.

Auster, P. (1987). City of Glass. New York, NY: Penguin Books.

Leo XIV. (2026). Magnifica Humanitas: On Safeguarding the Human Person in the Time of Artificial Intelligence. Encyclical letter. The Holy See.

#4707. Getting More Physical Activity May Help With Your Perimenopause Symptoms

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A new study found that exercising more frequently may help alleviate perimenopause symptoms like hot flashes, anxiety, and urinary issues.

The study results were recently presented at The Menopause Society’s 2026 Annual Conference.

Perimenopause is the transitional period leading up to menopause.

Due to hormonal changes that mark the end of a person’s reproductive years, symptoms like hot flashes, mood swings, brain fog, insomnia, and urinary incontinence are common.

Past studies show that lifestyle modifications, such as eating a healthy diet, managing stress, and getting enough physical activity, can help reduce some perimenopause symptoms.

“Physical activity is low cost, accessible, and already known to benefit sleep, mood, and heart and bone health — all areas that matter a great deal during perimenopause,” said study lead and co-author Liudmila Zhaunova, PhD, director of science at Flo Health — the developer of a women’s health tracking app, which was used to collect health data for this study. “But when we looked at the research, there was surprisingly little evidence specific to perimenopause.”

“Hormone therapy isn’t suitable or desired for everyone, so women deserve a broader set of evidence-based options,” Zhaunova told Healthline. “The more we understand about accessible, lifestyle-based approaches, the better equipped women and their healthcare providers are to build a plan that works for them.”

Study researchers recruited more than 1,800 women from around the globe who were using the Flo app.

Study participants were asked to complete online surveys about their physical activity, from not being physically active to exercising more than 5 days a week.

Participants were also asked to report on their perimenopause symptoms in three categories — somatic (body-based issues like hot flashes), psychological (mental health issues like mood changes), and urogenital (issues regarding the urinary or vaginal areas). Researchers rated the severity of these symptoms using the Menopause Rating Scale (MRS).

The researchers found that higher rates of physical activity were associated with fewer perimenopausal symptoms across all three categories.

“Perimenopause symptoms are wide-ranging, and women often experience several at once,” Zhaunova said. “Seeing a lower symptom burden across all three domains suggests that being more active may be relevant to women’s overall experience, not just one symptom.”

Additionally, the scientists discovered that the greatest exercise benefit was observed in the reduction of perimenopausal psychological symptoms.

“Psychological symptoms, such as low mood, irritability, anxiety, and exhaustion, are among the most disruptive parts of perimenopause, and they’re often overlooked or not recognized as related to this life stage,” Zhaunova explained.

“Our findings suggest that physical activity may matter most for mood and anxiety-related symptoms,” she continued.

“This could help women and clinicians have more informed conversations about how to support mental well-being during perimenopause. That said, women with more symptoms may find it harder to exercise, so we need further research to understand the direction of the relationship.”

Sherry Ross, MD, a board certified OB-GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, said that regular exercise could potentially help relieve perimenopause symptoms like hot flashes and mood changes. Ross wasn’t involved in this study, but noted other benefits of exercising during this life stage:

“Exercise releases endorphins, improves blood vessel health, lowers inflammation, helps reset circadian rhythm, and improves the body’s internal cooling system,” Ross told Healthline. “Collectively, these changes ease anxiety, irritability, mood changes, sleep, and fatigue.”

“There were mixed reviews on how exercise benefits hot flashes, but exercise does help with weight control, which may benefit hot flashes,” she said. “Strengthening the pelvic floor and core may help with the urinary symptoms women many experience in perimenopause.”

Prudence Hall, MD, an OB-GYN in private practice in Santa Monica, CA, and author of “Radiant Again & Forever,” said that building a sustainable exercise routine requires consistency, joy, and community. Hall wasn’t involved in the study, but shared some exercise tips for perimenopausal women.

“Too often in midlife, previously stable women suddenly plummet into deep depression and anxiety, only to be prescribed multiple medications with debilitating side effects that never address the underlying biology,” Hall said.

“While hormone optimization remains essential to correct these endocrine deficiencies, exercise serves as a powerful, non-pharmaceutical therapy that directly targets the true root causes by revitalizing our cellular health and restoring overall vitality.”

#4706. I Tried Adding 10 Minutes of Daily Mobility to My Routine for Two Weeks. Here’s How My Body—And Mind—Changed

Plus, the expert-backed reason a few minutes of mobility can add up over time.

I’m in my early 30s, which means staying fit requires more of a conscious, consistent effort. The natural loss of lean muscle mass and skin elasticity that occurs at this stage of life makes me more mindful of my body and overall well-being. So, I’ve declared this my year of wellness. As part of it, I have been working on adding small bouts of movement that manageably fit into my daily life. Mobility work felt like one of the best ways to do that.

Mobility is an incredibly underrated training modality, yet it’s an essential part of healthy aging—especially for those like me who spend most of the day sitting at a desk. Mobility training focuses on controlled, active movement through a joint’s full range of motion, says Matthew Cifelli, PT, DPT, CSCS, of Attain Physical Therapy.

This style of movement helps you perform nearly every daily task, from climbing stairs and getting up from a seated position to walking with a full stride and turning your head while driving. But as you age or spend extended periods of time being sedentary, it’s common for muscles to tighten, joints to stiffen, and movement to become less efficient.

“Limited mobility forces the body to compensate with inefficient patterns, increasing the risk of pain, balance issues, and injury,” says Cifelli. Maintaining mobility, on the other hand, “supports independence, joint health, and the ability to move confidently through life.”

That’s why I recently decided to add just 10 minutes of mobility work to my daily routine for two weeks. Here’s exactly what I did—and how my body changed.

Mobility is “not just about ‘feeling loose,’” says Cifelli. “It's about teaching the body to use its flexibility in real movement.” It’s a mix of static stretching and flexibility work that focuses on muscle length. “Mobility training targets how well a joint moves and how well you control that motion, which requires coordinated muscle activation and joint stability.”

And just a few minutes a day of mobility work can help boost circulation, lubricate the joints, alleviate muscle tension, and improve confidence in daily movement. “Even short sessions, when done daily, create meaningful cumulative change,” he says.

My routine included a combination of exercises and hold times I learned from Portia Page, CPT, in addition to a couple of stretches my physical therapist recommended incorporating into my home regimen. I performed each exercise for one minute, one time through.

During the first week of my experiment, I eased into my 10-minute mobility routine. I was eager to see how it could help improve my “desk body,” a.k.a. tight hips, tense hamstrings, and lower back and neck tension.

I did the workout every morning around 8 a.m. before diving into the madness of the day. It was pretty seamless to add to my mornings, since I have a dedicated workout space in my home, though the routine doesn’t require much space or equipment. Plus, I’m someone who craves routine. Sticking to the same time each morning made this fitness habit sustainable.

From the get-go, it was clear my body was tense and in desperate need of some stretching and mobility work. My legs, back, and hips all felt stiff at the beginning of the workout. Certain exercises, like the standing forward fold, hip flexor stretch, and supine figure-four stretch were more challenging than the rest. For example, during the first week, I found it difficult to touch the floor when doing the forward fold, so I didn’t force it.

By the end of each session, my body was definitely a bit more relaxed, but I knew I needed to stick with mobility work for more than just a week or two in order to achieve meaningful, lasting results.

I was a dancer growing up, and my body was much more flexible then than it is now. While the Pilates classes I attend three to four times a week have definitely helped me stretch and strengthen my body, a dedicated mobility routine felt like exactly what the doctor ordered. I didn’t realize it would help me in my classes, too. By the end of week one, I felt I was able to move through a more seamless range of motion in certain Pilates exercises like the mermaid and the straight-back hinge on the short box.

Heading into week two, I found myself looking forward to my morning mobility session. It started to feel like more of a natural segue into my day, similar to brushing my teeth, taking my vitamins, or getting dressed. Once I wrapped up stretching and sat down at my desk, my body felt more limber and relaxed as I started work. However, after a couple hours of sitting, I felt much more tense again. The experiment taught me to be mindful of that: My body needs movement throughout the day—not just first thing in the morning.

I felt inspired by this healthy mobility habit and how great I feel afterward, so I wanted to keep the momentum going. During week two, I started building other healthy habits, like getting up to walk around my kitchen and living room every hour and going on a longer brisk walk at the end of the day. Both helped me stay limber throughout the day, rather than just in the morning. My hope is that, with all of these bouts of movement combined, sitting won’t undo all of the wonderful benefits I get from my stretching routine.

By the end of the second week, I was pleased that my body felt more accustomed to the dedicated mobility work than it had during week one. The more challenging stretches also became slightly easier, which made me feel like I was making genuine progress.

The routine became a no-brainer—a staple, if you will—in my morning routine: I’d wake up, brew a soothing latte, and get to work on my yoga mat. It also sparked the desire to get up and move more during the workday rather than remain hunched over my laptop for an extended period of time.

Because I experienced the tension-relieving benefits of this mobility work almost immediately after each session during week two, I’m now inspired to do it at both the start and end of my day. It’s a great way to ease any built-up stiffness after a long day at my desk before slipping into bed.

That said, one thing I’d love to continue working on is my posture. I didn’t experience any groundbreaking improvements during this two-week timeframe, but I’m hopeful that I’ll make progress down the line. I’m also curious to see whether being consistent with this mobility routine long-term will help my body—especially my hips and lower back—feel less stiff after sitting or lounging for longer periods.

Consistency is key. As with any workout, consistency is essential for success. But alas, it’s something I’ve struggled with over the years. Hectic work weeks filled with deadlines and appointments typically push my fitness to the back burner.

However, during this two-week test period, I was incredibly determined to carve out 10 minutes each day for my stretching regimen, and I’m so glad I did. Sticking with this fitness habit helped me feel better mentally and physically. My body started to feel more flexible and limber by the end of the two-week period—something I don’t think I would have experienced if I were inconsistent with my efforts.

According to Page, a mere 5 to 10 minutes a day of mobility work can make a noticeable difference over time if you’re consistent with the habit. She recommends thinking of stretching “not as a luxury but as basic maintenance for your body—like brushing your teeth.”

Kickstarting the day with fitness can promote other healthy habits. Starting the day with mobility work inspired me to follow other healthy habits throughout. After all, I was already off to a solid start and wanted to keep that momentum going strong.

Following each mobility session, I felt accomplished, energized, and ready to tackle the day. I found myself sticking with my regular Pilates workouts, making all-around healthier meal choices, snacking less, and adding brief “movement snacks” to my afternoons to break up the time spent sitting at my desk.

Mobility is a low-barrier starting point for movement. What I love best about this mobility workout? I don’t need to leave the comfort of my home or have access to fancy equipment. I’ve seamlessly incorporated these exercises into my self-care routine, and it just takes 10 minutes of my morning before I dive into work deadlines and commitments.

While there’s always room for improvement—and I’d like to add even more stretches to my routine—I felt incredibly accomplished overall with only a 10-minute routine. I’m hopeful that, by starting now and being consistent with mobility training, I can help prepare my body to tackle everyday tasks with ease. This training can also help me stay mobile, confident, and independent in my adventurous lifestyle for the long term.

Alexa is a content strategist, editor, and writer based in Greenwich, Connecticut, who has more than 12 years of experience writing for travel, lifestyle, and fitness publications. Alexa’s work has appeared in Business Insider, Parade, Men's Journal, Apartment Therapy, Men’s Fitness, Allrecipes, Family Handyman, Eat This, Not That!, Body Network, Everyday Health, SheBuysTravel, Tasting Table, Elite Daily, and more. When she’s not writing, you’ll likely find her at Pilates, hiking, designing her next tablescape, or jetting off on a getaway.

#4705. BYD is going all out on its ultra-luxury EV with coach doors and 1,000+ km of range [Images]

BYD unveiled the Yangwang Altior, its new ultra-luxury EV with coach doors, over 1,000 km of CTLC range, a 1,000V fast-charging platform, and plenty of premium extras.

The “super-luxury executive flagship sedan,” as BYD calls it, made its official debut in Abu Dhabi, UAE, over the weekend.

For those who don’t know, Yangwang is BYD’s ultra-luxury sub-brand, sitting at the very top of its brand hierarchy.

The Atrio is Yangwang’s largest and most luxurious sedan, set to compete with high-end brands like Rolls-Royce, Bentley, and Mercedes-Benz Maybach.

Measuring 5,600 mm long, 2,030 mm wide, and 1,590 mm tall, with a 3,500 mm wheelbase, BYD’s flagship sedan sits squarely between the Rolls-Royce Ghost and Phantom (standard wheelbase) in length.

BYD said the “Golden Body Proportions” are designed to maximize interior space for both front and rear passengers.

Its meticulous front-end design is inspired by “Ding,” a traditional ancient Chinese cauldron, featuring “diamond-cut” headlights, a 137-gemstone dot-matrix grille, and, to top it off, a 24K pure gold car emblem sits up front and center.

The coach doors create a grand entrance, with the front doors opening at an 80-degree angle and the rear doors opening to a 90-degree angle.

Inside, the flagship sedan takes luxury up a notch with a massive, full-length panoramic center infotainment screen that extends from the driver to the passenger side.

The “Wrap-around cockpit” is designed to create an immersive, premium experience, with four executive seats and a central island for rear passengers that includes vehicle controls, storage, and even a champagne glass holder.

BYD said it offers the most second-row space in its class, but didn’t reveal specifics. The zero-gravity “cloud-like” rear seats feature a four-ball mechanical massage head, you know, for those longer trips.

Meanwhile, the front passenger seat can fold at the push of a button to open up more space for rear passengers.

The interior features premium materials, including full-grain genuine leather seats, diamond-cut detailing, real wood trim, and natural lambswool foot pads.

And that’s not all. It also has a 39-speaker Dynaudio Platinum Evidence high-end sound system that creates an immersive 360-degree “hall-level” sound experience.

The Yangwang Altio is packed with BYD’s latest breakthrough tech, including a high-speed tire-blowout stability system, emergency float mode, and in-place U-turn or tank-turn control using its quad-motor e4 platform.

It's main rival is the Maextro S800, which wasn't in the list.

It also uses BYD’s second-generation Blade Batteries and Fast Charging Technology, which provides a CLTC driving range of over 1,000 km (621 miles).

The flagship sedan features “extremely fast flash charging,” BYD said, thanks to its 1000V ultra flash charging tech. It takes just five minutes to charge the vehicle’s battery from 10% to 70%. To go from 10% to 97% it takes just nine minutes.

BYD opened orders for the limited-edition “Mountain and River Rhyme” Yangwang Altrio model, which will be extremely exclusive with just 399 units.

Buyers can place a reservation with a 300,000 yuan ($45,000) deposit. BYD didn’t reveal final prices, but the global version is expected to start at around 2 million yuan ($300,000).
